Air Canada Aeroplan — Partner Awards with Stopovers

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 16 min read (3183 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

⏱️ ~16 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.
  • The only major program offering free stopovers on one-way partner awards.
  • ## Flying Business Class Across Two Continents for the Price of One Imagine settling into a fully flat bed on a Boeing 787-9 somewhere over the Pacific, a warm towel in your hand, Japan behind you and Singapore ahead.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

The only major program offering free stopovers on one-way partner awards.

## Flying Business Class Across Two Continents for the Price of One Imagine settling into a fully flat bed on a Boeing 787-9 somewhere over the Pacific, a warm towel in your hand, Japan behind you and Singapore ahead. You've already spent three days eating ramen in Tokyo — a stopover you added to your award ticket for a mere 5,000 extra points. This isn't a once-in-a-lifetime splurge. This is what the ChooseFI community calls a **nearly free** trip, engineered through one of the most underappreciated sweet spots in the entire travel rewards ecosystem. The Air Canada Aeroplan stopover rule is genuinely one of the last great loopholes in loyalty travel. Here's the math that makes your jaw drop: a business class flight from Toronto to Singapore — routed through Tokyo with a multi-day stopover — retails for **$8,000 to $10,000 in cash**. You can book that same itinerary for **70,000 Aeroplan points** (plus 5,000 for the stopover, so 75,000 total). At a conservative cash value of $8,000, you're extracting **10.7 cents per point** — more than double what most programs offer, and squarely within Aeroplan's documented range of **5.7 to 14.3 cents per point**. To put that in FI terms: if you value your points at even the low end of that range — 5.7 cents per point — 75,000 Aeroplan points are worth **$4,275 in travel**. At the high end, you're looking at **$10,725**. That's a portfolio-level return on the credit card spending and transfer partners you've already been accumulating. What makes this feel different from other premium redemptions is the *shape* of the trip itself. You're not just flying business class — you're building a mini round-the-world itinerary. Tokyo and Singapore in the same award ticket. Two of the world's great cities. Two business class flights. One redemption. The inefficiency here isn't accidental — it's baked into how Aeroplan prices stopovers at a flat 5,000 miles, regardless of where you stop. The program is essentially inviting you to stack experiences on a single award, and the ChooseFI community is the group paying close enough attention to accept that invitation.

The core insight is this: Air Canada Aeroplan uses a fixed partner award chart for Star Alliance flights, and it prices stopovers at a flat 5,000-mile premium regardless of routing complexity. That single policy decision transforms a standard business class award into a multi-destination adventure at a fraction of the combined retail cost.

In a recent development, here's the mechanism. When Aeroplan relaunched in 2020, it did something most programs had abandoned years earlier: it kept a fixed-rate award chart for partner airlines. While programs like United MileagePlus moved to fully dynamic pricing — where award costs fluctuate with demand — Aeroplan locked in predictable rates for Star Alliance partners. The YYZ to SIN corridor in business class sits at a rate that reflects the geography, not the current demand spike or revenue management algorithm. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community can systematically exploit.

Sources indicate that layer on top of that the stopover rule: Aeroplan allows one free stopover on one-way partner awards for just 5,000 additional miles. A stopover is defined as a connection of more than 24 hours. So your Toronto → Tokyo → Singapore routing becomes a Toronto → Tokyo (stopover 3 days) → Singapore itinerary, all on one award ticket, for 75,000 points total. You've essentially purchased two separate international business class flights for the price of one, plus a nominal surcharge.

The other critical piece: Aeroplan charges zero fuel surcharges on partner awards. This was a deliberate policy decision in the 2020 relaunch and it's a massive advantage. Programs like British Airways Avios and Singapore KrisFlyer can add $500–$1,500 in surcharges to long-haul business class awards. With Aeroplan, you pay government taxes only — typically $50–$150 on most itineraries.

Recent findings suggest that you don't need to fly Air Canada or hold an Air Canada credit card to access this. Aeroplan accepts transfers from several major flexible currency programs at a 1:1 ratio:.

Chase Ultimate Rewards is your best friend here because transfers are instant, which matters when you're racing to book a specific award seat before someone else claims it. If you hold a Chase Sapphire Preferred, Chase Sapphire Reserve, or Ink Business Preferred, your UR points can become Aeroplan points in seconds.

Sources indicate that the booking window is 355 days out, which gives you nearly a full year of planning runway — a significant advantage for families coordinating schedules or travelers targeting peak periods in Tokyo or Singapore. Partner award availability on Aeroplan is generally solid for the Star Alliance network, with business class seats on ANA, Japan Airlines (where applicable), and Singapore Airlines routes opening up regularly. Availability scores a 4 out of 5 for this sweet spot, which reflects genuine accessibility rather than theoretical possibility.

Never transfer points until you have confirmed, bookable award space in hand. Go to aeroplan.com and use the flight search tool. Select "Business" class, enter your origin and destination (e.g., Toronto YYZ to Singapore SIN), and search for one-way awards. Aeroplan's search engine will show you available partner space directly — you don't need a separate search on partner airline websites, though checking ana.co.jp or singaporeair.com for business class availability can help you triangulate what's open before logging into Aeroplan.

It has been revealed that look for awards showing Star Alliance partner carriers (ANA, Singapore Airlines, and others depending on routing). The system will display the points cost and any routing options. Aeroplan's booking window opens 355 days in advance, so set a calendar reminder to search the moment your target travel window becomes available.

Recent findings suggest that once you've found an outbound flight you like (e.g., Toronto → Tokyo), call Aeroplan at 1-800-361-5373 or use the online multi-city search to add a stopover at your midpoint city. A stopover is any connection exceeding 24 hours. The system will add 5,000 points to your base award cost. Confirm the full itinerary indicates both the Tokyo stopover segment and the onward Tokyo → Singapore flight in the cabin class you want.

Note: Online booking for complex multi-city awards with stopovers sometimes requires a phone call to complete. Budget 30–45 minutes for the call and have your routing clearly written out before you dial.

Sources indicate that if using Amex Membership Rewards, Capital One, or Bilt, initiate the transfer and expect a 1–2 day processing window. Have your Aeroplan member number ready. Do NOT transfer until you've confirmed availability in Step 1.

Sources indicate that once your points land in your Aeroplan account, return to aeroplan.com and complete the booking within the same browser session if possible. Pay the government taxes and fees with a credit card that earns rewards on travel purchases. Taxes on a routing like YYZ → NRT → SIN are typically in the $100–$200 range — no fuel surcharges.

After booking, download or screenshot your itinerary confirmation. Verify the cabin class on each segment. Check in on the Aeroplan website 24 hours before each flight and confirm your seat assignments. For the stopover city, you are responsible for your own accommodation — budget accordingly, and consider this the best "forced layover" you'll ever take.

A stopover is a deliberate break in your journey at a connecting city, where you stay for more than 24 hours before continuing to your final destination. Most loyalty programs treat stopovers as separate tickets, requiring you to pay miles for each segment independently. Aeroplan breaks this convention by allowing one free stopover on one-way awards, meaning your connecting city becomes a bonus destination at zero additional mileage cost. For example, a flight from Fresh York to Tokyo with a 5-day stopover in Istanbul costs the same 75,000 Aeroplan points as flying directly — but you get to explore Istanbul for nearly a week as part of the trip. The stopover must be at a connection point that makes geographic sense for your routing, but with 26+ Star Alliance airlines and hundreds of hub cities, the options are vast.

Sources indicate that card links may earn ChooseFI a commission. See our advertiser disclosure.

Let's build out a specific redemption so the math becomes undeniable.

The Itinerary: You depart Toronto Pearson (YYZ) on an ANA Boeing 787-9 bound for Tokyo Narita (NRT). You've built in a 3-day stopover in Tokyo — enough time for a morning at Tsukiji, an evening in Shinjuku, and a day trip to Nikko. Then you board a Singapore Airlines flight from NRT to Singapore Changi (SIN) in Business Class.

The Cash Price: A business class itinerary covering this exact routing — YYZ to NRT to SIN — retails in the range of $8,000 to $10,000, depending on season and carrier. Booking two separate one-way tickets (YYZ-NRT and NRT-SIN) in business class would easily exceed that, often landing closer to $10,000–$12,000 combined.

The Points Cost: 70,000 Aeroplan points for the base award + 5,000 for the stopover = 75,000 points total, plus approximately $120–$180 in government taxes. No fuel surcharges.

According to recent reports, the CPP Calculation: At a midpoint cash value of $9,000, your 75,000 points are generating 12 cents per point. Even at the conservative $8,000 end, you're at 10.7 cents per point — well within the documented 5.7–14.3 cent range and significantly above the ChooseFI rule of thumb of 2 cents per point for most redemptions.

What You're Actually Experiencing:.

Industry observers note that on the ANA 787-9 YYZ–NRT segment, you're in ANA's Business Staggered seat — a fully flat bed with direct aisle access, Japanese hospitality, and one of the best business class dining experiences in the sky. The Tokyo stopover is yours to explore however you like. Then Singapore Airlines' Business Class on the NRT–SIN leg offers its own benchmark product — a refined seat, excellent service, and arrival into Changi, consistently ranked the world's best airport.

You've visited two of Asia's most celebrated cities, flown on two world-class airlines, slept flat across the Pacific, and your out-of-pocket cash cost was under $200. That is the ChooseFI travel rewards mindset in its purest form.

Aeroplan allows open jaw routing. You can fly INTO Tokyo and OUT of Singapore on separate awards, pairing this business class redemption with a separate economy or business award home. Build your Southeast Asia trip so you land in one city and depart from another — no backtracking, better geography, same award pricing framework.

Recent findings suggest that this is the single most common mistake in all of travel rewards. If you transfer 75,000 Chase UR to Aeroplan and then discover the award space disappeared, you cannot transfer back. Chase points are gone. Confirm bookable space first, transfer second, book third.

The Chase Sapphire Reserve earns 3x on travel and dining. The Amex Platinum earns 5x on flights booked directly. Build your Aeroplan balance through the transfer partners rather than flying Air Canada itself — the flexibility is far more valuable.

It has been revealed that this redemption is ideal for couples and solo travelers with a genuine interest in Asia — specifically anyone who has ever dreamed of Japan and Southeast Asia in the same trip without paying for two separate premium tickets. If your travel bucket list includes Tokyo and Singapore in the same itinerary, this is the single most efficient way to get there in business class.

Minimum points needed: ~75,000 Aeroplan points (70,000 base + 5,000 stopover). Build this through Chase UR, Amex MR, Capital One, or Bilt transfers.

For the FI-minded traveler, this is a high-ROI, low-cash-cost adventure that fits perfectly into a strategy of saving aggressively while experiencing the world nearly free.

## Why This Is Rated Moderate — And How to Handle It This sweet spot earns a **moderate difficulty** rating — not because the math is complicated, but because the booking process has more moving parts than a simple domestic award. **What makes it moderate:** 1. **Complex routing with a stopover** — Aeroplan's online tool doesn't always handle multi-city stopover bookings cleanly. You may need to call Aeroplan to finalize the itinerary, which adds a step and requires you to have your routing clearly planned before you dial. 2. **Partner award availability** — You're booking seats on ANA, Singapore Airlines, or other Star Alliance carriers, not Air Canada. Chase's instant transfer largely solves this problem. **Three tips to make it manageable:** - **Use aeroplan.com's multi-city search first** to understand what routing options exist before calling. Come to any phone call with a primary and backup itinerary already researched. - **Book 6–12 months out** using the 355-day window. More availability, more flexibility, less stress. - **Do one transfer before you need to** — move a small amount of points to Aeroplan just to practice the process and verify your accounts are linked. If you've successfully booked a domestic business class award before, this is a natural next step. No. The free stopover on a one-way award is included at no additional mileage cost. A flight from Latest York to Bangkok with a stopover in Istanbul costs the same as New York to Bangkok direct.

Aeroplan prices round trips as two one-way tickets. Each one-way award allows one free stopover, so a round-trip booking can include up to two stopovers — one on the outbound and one on the return. This effectively turns a round trip into a four-destination itinerary.

Lufthansa, Swiss, Austrian, and THAI Airways impose significant fuel surcharges on award tickets that can add $100 to $400 per segment. To minimize out-of-pocket costs, route through carriers with no or low surcharges: Turkish Airlines, ANA, EVA Air, Singapore Airlines (on most routes), and United. Check the fare breakdown before confirming your booking.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

In a recent development, aeroplan's free stopover on one-way awards is a genuinely unique feature that no other major North American loyalty program offers. The ability to spend a week in Istanbul, Singapore, or Tokyo as a free add-on to your business class award makes Aeroplan one of the most valuable programs in the travel rewards ecosystem. Combine this with access to 26+ Star Alliance carriers, online booking for stopover routings, and 1:1 transfers from Chase, Amex, Capital One, and Bilt, and you have a program that delivers outsized value for the ChooseFI community. Gliver completes the Guix desktop

📅 22 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1552 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Dustycloud

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • By Christine Lemmer-Webber on Sun 22 November 2026.
  • Industry observers note that there's a bit of irony in the title.
  • In a recent development, notably, that release will be 0.0.5.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Christine Lemmer-Webber on Sun 22 November 2026.

Industry observers note that there's a bit of irony in the title. At the time of writing, Gliver, a Guile based window manager for Wayland in the style of StumpWM and Emacs, isn't yet in Guix. There is, however, an open PR to add Gliver to Guix. However, what that patch is really waiting on is an upcoming release of Gliver which will solve many bugs.

In a recent development, notably, that release will be 0.0.5. If that sounds early, Gliver still is early. There are bugs, and you will probably have to file issues for some that you discover. There are also some noticeable missing features. But it doesn't matter. Gliver is everything I want from a desktop experience, and I suspect for many of the kinds of people who read my blog, it will be for them as well.

According to recent reports, gliver might not be for everyone. But if the following appeals to you: a live-hackable, written in Guile Scheme, tiling window manager which looks good, feels good, and whose codebase is understandable and, indeed, encourages you to understand and explore it, Gliver is for you.

I think Anna Liberty's Towards Understandable Software is a must-read. Call it a counter-vision to the vibe bobsled. Anna lays out that software should be more understandable, not less, and easy to participate in even for people with no programming background. While Gliver doesn't itself try all the approaches Anna lays out, it is an understandable codebase.

In a recent development, furthermore, Gliver is participatory. Gliver invites you to learn its internals and explore it. By default, Gliver's describe-key functionality opens a window where you can type the command you are thinking of, and it will show you what key it is bound to... but you can also type in a key sequence, and it'll show you what command that runs.

Industry observers note that more than that, by default Gliver opens a unix domain socket in ~/.local/state/gliver/repl.sock. You can connect to this, say with Geiser. You are live! You know that command you just looked up with the above describe-key interface? Why not try running it at the REPL! Hey, how does it work? Well Geiser already has a feature for that; by default typing M-. (geiser-edit-symbol-at-point) will jump you right to the definition, and you can explore how that code works! You can run commands manually at the REPL, you can inspect the state of the system, you can hack away, you can take the useful things you have learned and add them to your init.scm file so that the next time Gliver starts things are more the way you want them than last time. But of course there's no need to wait, this is a lisp style system! You can eval those changes and apply them immediately and carry on your way.

Maybe this all sounds pretty technical, and even technically elite. And I think Gliver is probably not very accessible to non-scheme-hackers. But on the other hand, it could help you become a Scheme hacker.

Industry observers note that when I started using Emacs, I was not a programmer. By extending Emacs, I became a programmer. (My background is not in CS; I was an interdisciplinary humanities student.) Emacs invites you to explore how it works by customizing it. My entire career would not have likely happened if Emacs did not welcome me into this process.

Sources indicate that gliver takes the same approach. But instead of Emacs Lisp, which is a hackable but honestly not really great lisp, it uses Guile Scheme, which is lovely. And notably, this is the same language as Guix.

According to recent reports, there is more I want to say on this, and I will in a future article. In many ways I think Blender is also an interesting example of reflective software in action, and actually does expose some of the ideas such as visual programming for non-programmers in a way that Emacs and Gliver don't, with great success too. But that's to discuss later.

But as for the choice to switch. I have gotten tired of using systems that feel like they know better than I do. I have spent most of my days using GNOME, but without getting too much into it, I have been burnt way too many times by a paternalistic attitude which seems at the center of its design philosophy. When I did the latest upgrade and found out that custom application launcher shortcuts did not work anymore, and I could not figure out for the life of me why, I decided I didn't actually care to try to solve the problem this time. I was going to try something else.

According to recent reports, which is when I re-discovered Gliver. Thanks to ebeem for working on Gliver and jfred for having been an earlier adopter than I was and who helped me with some messy this-isnt-yet-packaged trickiness.

I suppose I've already mentioned most of it, but a few more details. One interesting aspect of Gliver is that it uses River, which is a Wayland compositor which is designed as a framework for building window managers on top of. Building small window managers had become a lot harder to do with the move from X11 to Wayland; River provides a common foundation that makes it much more possible.

Gliver allegedly supports different tiling modes, but I don't use them, I just use manual tiling. I like splitting up my screens the way I like them. I know I want this thing here and that thing there. Gliver shines at this kind of manual flow. It also has multiple "tabbed" windows stacked in each pane of the frames (in Gliver, each of those panes is called a "container"). You can move around what workspace and container a window "belongs to" with keybindings. Personally I bound -x to be a keymapping with sub-bindings for splitting things up with the same equivalent keys as they are in emacs, since those mappings are burned into my brain.

It has been revealed that the default theme is very nice. You can customize its colors but black and purple is exactly my jam already.

There are some rough edges. I have filed a number of issues for the things I've encountered. But one of the most noticeable is that there are several commands you might find for launching shell commands or creating newly introduced workspaces where you would expect to be prompted. For example, here's one of Gliver's commands for running a shell command:.

Nice, these look like good commands, let's bind them to keys in our config! But oh wait, nothing happens! That's strange, they work at the REPL, why don't they work when bound to a key?

It has been revealed that the simple answer is that #:interactive (string) part you see above, which indicates that Gliver's UI should be asking you for a prompt and letting you type in something, simply isn't implemented yet! So when I say there are some missing features, there really are some missing features.

But this all may be changing very promptly. ebeem is working on a refactor of the GUI system to be more of a functional reactive programming type system, inspired by Flutter. When that lands, I expect a number of bugs to be fixed, and a number of missing features like the above to land.

According to recent reports, this does lead to the funny situation that to create a latest workspace, I have to do it at the REPL! That's okay. It'll be fixed, and for now, it's a nice reminder that running things at the REPL is something I can absolutely do at any time with Gliver, which I appreciate.

Speaking of the GUI, what GUI toolkit is it using, you may wonder? The answer is: it kind of has its own thing! Gliver has FFI bindings to Cairo for its vector graphics and Pango for fonts. That's it! It seems to be a good enough foundation for the rest it is using and doing.

Now, how am I running Gliver at all when it isn't in Guix? The funny thing is that for now, I am running out of a git checkout of Gliver. I start up and sacrifice the not-so-proverbial Cow window manager and replace it live with Gliver in a terminal like so:.

Which is basically the trick in the Gliver README, just starting with a cow sacrifice first. Pretty ugly though, it'll be nicer when Gliver is just packaged in Guix.

In a recent development, gliver is nice. It feels good, it works well. And it's participatory, understandable software. It's also very early. It might not be for everyone, but it has elements of a vision for a future I'd like to see for everyone.

In a recent development, if you like the idea of a scheme'y lisp machine using Guix as your operating system distribution but have found that the desktop experience was missing, well, Gliver is now here! And soon, packaged in a Guix near you.

And, I suspect, once it is... well, we'll be seeing most of the Guix community moving over. It's too exciting and too nice not to!

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that some numbers are hard to picture until you sit with them for a moment. Last week we published the Prime Day 2026 metrics, and the one that stuck with me is 2.3 quadrillion: the daily requests Amazon ElastiCache peaked at during the event. Prime Day ran back in June, so this post always lands as a retrospective, and that gap is part of what makes it worth reading. By the time the numbers reach you, the only evidence that any of it happened is that nothing went wrong.

Sources indicate that the rest of the week pulled in a different direction: smaller, cheaper, and more constrained. Claude Haiku 5.5 arrived on Amazon Bedrock at roughly 75 percent less than Haiku 4.5, Amazon Nova 2.5 Sonic made voice agents quicker on their feet, and Strands Box revealed up to put real boundaries around what an agent is allowed to do. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

HeadlinesAll the numbers: Amazon Prime Day 2026 powered by AWS is the latest entry in a tradition that goes back to 2016, and the scale is still difficult to hold in your head. Over the four days of Prime Day, Amazon DynamoDB processed more than 59 trillion requests while peaking at 192 million requests per second, and kept single-digit millisecond responses throughout. AWS Lambda handled over 2.3 trillion invocations per day. Amazon EBS peaked above 24.8 trillion I/O operations, moving more than an exabyte of data daily. Amazon ECS launched an average of 158.3 million tasks per day on AWS Fargate, a 47.7 percent jump over last year, and AWS Graviton powered up to 49 percent of the Amazon EC2 compute that Amazon.com used.

In a recent development, the number I keep coming back to, though, isn’t a throughput record. The team ran more than 44,000 AWS Fault Injection Service experiments ahead of the event, more than six times what they ran in 2025. Those are deliberate failures injected on purpose, months in advance, so that the trillions of requests above turn into an ordinary shopping afternoon. If you’re preparing for your own peak moment, AWS Countdown Premium is built for exactly that kind of planning.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Developers building web and AI applications on Vercel can now add Amazon S3 storage resources directly from the Vercel Marketplace and v0, combining the durability, scalability, and performance of S3 with the convenience of Vercel’s provisioning workflow.
  • Sources indicate that why this matters Millions of developers build, deploy, and scale web and AI applications on Vercel.
  • In a recent development, getting started From the Vercel dashboard, go to the Storage tab and choose Create.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Developers building web and AI applications on Vercel can now add Amazon S3 storage resources directly from the Vercel Marketplace and v0, combining the durability, scalability, and performance of S3 with the convenience of Vercel’s provisioning workflow. Starting today, Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), including Amazon S3 Tables and Amazon S3 Vectors, is natively available on the Vercel Marketplace and v0 by Vercel, covering three distinct workloads: everyday storage, analytics, and AI.

Sources indicate that why this matters Millions of developers build, deploy, and scale web and AI applications on Vercel. Storage is essential to performant applications, but provisioning it previously required navigating to the AWS Management Console to configure policies and credentials. Now, S3 storage integrates directly into the Vercel developer experience, with resource provisioning and connection configuration handled automatically. Together with existing integrations for Amazon Aurora, Amazon DynamoDB, and Amazon OpenSearch Serverless, you get a complete application stack inside Vercel (from your database layer through to object, vector, and open table storage), all on one AWS account with one bill.

Figure 1 – The AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace.

In a recent development, getting started From the Vercel dashboard, go to the Storage tab and choose Create. Select AWS, pick your S3 bucket type, choose a Region, and create the bucket. Provisioning takes a few seconds.

Figure 2 – Creating an Amazon S3 general purpose bucket in Vercel by choosing a Region and a name.

Connect the bucket to a project, then pull the environment variables with the Vercel CLI:.

In a recent development, the integration injects AWS_REGION, AWS_ROLE_ARN, AWS_RESOURCE_ARN, and a bucket name such as S3_BUCKET_NAME, S3_TABLE_BUCKET_NAME, or S3_VECTOR_BUCKET_NAME. At runtime, the awsCredentialsProvider from @vercel/functions/oidc exchanges a short-lived OIDC token with AWS Security Token Service (AWS STS) for temporary credentials scoped to your resource. No static keys are stored anywhere.

Object storage with S3 This Next.js route uploads a file to a general purpose bucket:.

Use ListObjectsV2Command and GetObjectCommand with the same client to list and read objects.

Recent findings suggest that analytics with S3 Tables S3 Tables offer S3 storage purpose-built for analytics and are designed to automatically optimize query performance as data volumes grow. They provide fully managed Apache Iceberg tables with automated table maintenance and compaction, and they work with any Apache Iceberg REST Catalog-compliant engine. You can use DuckDB inside a Vercel Function for lightweight queries. This example attaches the table bucket by its ARN and runs an aggregate query:.

If you run DuckDB inside a Next.js route, add @duckdb/node-api to serverExternalPackages in next.config.mjs so the native bindings are not bundled.

Vector search with S3 Vectors S3 Vectors deliver purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage for AI agents, AI inference, and semantic search of your content stored in Amazon S3. S3 Vectors provides native support for storing and querying vectors without a separate vector database, but it does not generate them. Create the embeddings with your model of choice, then query the index for the closest matches:.

Building with v0 by Vercel From v0, describe what you want to build and it provisions the right resource. Ask for “a photo gallery where customers upload images using AWS” to get a general purpose bucket, “a support bot that answers questions from my PDFs” to get S3 Vectors, or “an analytics dashboard for my clickstream data” to get S3 Tables. v0 then configures the connection and generates working code.

Figure 3 – v0 generating a PDF support bot from a natural language prompt, with Amazon S3 Vectors connected and the application in the Preview panel.

Industry observers note that combining S3 with AWS databases Every AWS service on Vercel shares the same account and authentication model, so you can combine them with no extra setup. For example, store file metadata in Aurora with the files in S3, or store document text in DynamoDB with embeddings in S3 Vectors for RAG retrieval.

It has been revealed that using Vercel with your AWS account You can create a upcoming AWS account through the integration, which supports S3 features for building and testing. You can also link an existing AWS account to use your full set of S3 and AWS capabilities and keep your current billing. If you link an existing AWS account, Vercel works only with new buckets that you create through the platform. Because every S3 resource lives in your own AWS account, you keep AWS-native tooling and a single place to manage storage.

Pricing and availability There is no charge for the integration, and you pay standard Amazon S3 pricing for the resources you use. Latest AWS accounts created through Vercel receive $100 in credits valid for six months. Amazon S3, including S3 Tables and S3 Vectors, is available from v0 and the Vercel Marketplace in all commercial AWS Regions supported by Vercel. To get started, visit v0 or the AWS page on the Vercel Marketplace.

They're designed to play well together:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that nothing last week added a new kind of compute.
  • In a recent development, the counterweight arrived on Thursday.
  • Sources indicate that headlinesAWS Lambda Web Functions is a new form factor that runs a standard HTTP web application on Lambda without rewriting it into an event handler.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that nothing last week added a new kind of compute. What it did instead was shorten the distance between the code you already have and that code being live. AWS Lambda learned to run a plain HTTP server with no adapter in front of it, and Amazon S3 became something you can provision from inside the tool you were already using, without opening the AWS Management Console. Different services, same direction.

In a recent development, the counterweight arrived on Thursday. As it gets easier to put things into production, it matters more that you can say what those things are allowed to do, and this week’s most interesting read is about exactly that. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

Sources indicate that headlinesAWS Lambda Web Functions is a new form factor that runs a standard HTTP web application on Lambda without rewriting it into an event handler. You take a port-listening server built with Express, Hono, Fastify, or Next.js, run aws lambda-web deploy, and get back a live HTTPS URL in under a minute. No adapters, no infrastructure to set up first, no framework lock-in. Lambda now has three form factors on the same Firecracker isolation, which compose inside one application: Event Functions (the model you already know) for async work, Web Functions for the user-facing layer, and MicroVMs for stateful sandboxes running untrusted code.

In a recent development, two details make this more than repackaging. Each execution environment handles up to 128 concurrent requests, so a burst of traffic shares warm environments instead of mapping one request to one environment, and billing meters the CPU time your code actually uses rather than wall-clock time. For server-side rendering, API backends, and inference endpoints streaming tokens, where most of the elapsed time is spent waiting, that changes the arithmetic. Adding --regions to the same deploy command replicates your code and configures latency-based routing behind a single global URL, and you can split traffic across revisions by weight for a canary rollout. It’s available in five Regions, running Node.js 24 on Arm64 with VPC connectivity. The AWS Compute Blog has a longer walkthrough, and Amazon CloudFront can now use a Web Function endpoint as an origin with origin access control.

It has been revealed that the week’s other headline isn’t a launch. Trust in Depth: giving agents more autonomy without losing control makes an argument I keep running into in practice: putting a person in the loop for every agent action works at small scale and then quietly stops working, because people asked to check everything stop catching what matters. The alternative is four questions answered at four moments, which AWS calls scope, know, bound, and observe. The part worth sitting with is that an agent’s limits belong outside its own reasoning, in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore policies enforced at the gateway, because an agent cannot turn off a control it does not run. AWS has run automated reasoning in production for more than a decade, including AWS Identity and Access Management at more than 2.1 billion requests per second, and the case here is for pointing it at the rules you write for agents.

📅 20 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (877 w)

Industry News: Introducing Amazon ECS Gateway: A fully-managed ingress solution for ECS services

📅 20 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (877 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, when platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck.
  • Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.
  • ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, when platform teams manage containerized applications at scale on Amazon Elastic Container Service (Amazon ECS), configuring ingress networking for each service often becomes a bottleneck. For every new service, teams must provision and connect Application Load Balancers (ALBs), AWS Certificate Manager (ACM) certificates, AWS WAF web ACLs, and security groups, then keep those resources in sync as services scale, update, or operate. This per-service overhead slows down deployment velocity and increases the risk of configuration drift across an organization.

Today, we’re announcing Amazon ECS Gateway, a new account-level resource that simplifies ingress networking for containerized workloads by dynamically provisioning and managing the necessary infrastructure on your behalf, with all resources created directly in your account.

ECS Gateway introduces a clear separation of responsibilities between platform teams and application teams.

ECS Gateway offers host-based routing using ALBs and enables up to 25 services to share a single ALB, optimizing infrastructure costs. ECS manages the full lifecycle of the underlying infrastructure, provisioning the first ALB when your first service connects, adding more ALBs as capacity is reached, and removing them when no longer needed. Each service receives a unique DNS hostname, giving your teams a ready-to-use endpoint the moment provisioning completes.

Industry observers note that A first look at ECS Gateway In the ECS console, platform team can create a gateway and sets its configuration. The infrastructure role is an IAM role that ECS assumes to provision and manage networking resources such as ALBs, security groups, and certificates in your account. To create a gateway, provide a gateway name and select an infrastructure role. You can optionally associate the gateway with ECS clusters during creation or later.

Sources indicate that choose a load balancing scheme, either public or VPC-internal traffic routing. Under Additional Settings, you can also set up a listener, port, maximum count of load balancers the gateway can scale to, and a web ACL lets you protect your web applications. Some settings, including the name, scheme, VPC, subnets, IP address type, listener protocol and port cannot be changed after gateway creation.

Using AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), call CreateGateway with a name (unique per account), an infrastructure role, and a configuration object. No infrastructure is provisioned until a service connects with a gateway connector.

Once the gateway is created, you can take a look at the detailed configuration, gateway routes, load balancers, and associated clusters.

Now associate the gateway with one or more clusters (many-to-many), to make it available to ECS services on those clusters.

Use AssociateGatewayWithCluster to make the gateway available to services on a cluster:.

According to recent reports, to create and manage the ECS Gateway programmatically, including calling APIs and searching documentation, try the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI coding tool. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Gateway documentation.

ECS Gateway:Behind the scenesA gateway can be associated with up to 10,000 clusters, and a single cluster supports up to five gateway associations. This many-to-many relationship gives platform teams the flexibility to share a gateway across environments or assign multiple gateways (for example, public and private) to a single cluster.

Recent findings suggest that platform teams can control access by choosing which gateways to associate with which clusters. For additional control, use IAM policies to restrict who can deploy services to specific clusters.

Application teams add the gateway connector to each service definition in CreateService or UpdateService. If you have an existing ECS service with its own load balancer, you can adopt ECS Gateway incrementally by calling UpdateService to add a gateway connector. Both ingress paths remain available, allowing you to validate the gateway connection before removing the existing load balancer configuration.

It has been revealed that at deployment time, Amazon ECS evaluates the gateways associated with the cluster and connects the service to every compatible gateway. A gateway is compatible when its access type matches the service’s connector filter, it is in the same VPC as the service, and it covers all Availability Zones used by the service’s configured subnets.

For each connection, Amazon ECS assigns the service to an ALB with available capacity and provisions the per-service resources: an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, a listener rule routing traffic for that hostname to the service target group, and a service security group allowing inbound traffic only from the ALB security group. If no existing ALB has capacity, ECS creates a new one (up to maxAlbCount referring to quota limit). Once provisioning completes, the gateway route becomes ACTIVE, and the service URL is ready to receive traffic.

ECS Gateway handles common operational scenarios automatically:.

Things to Know Here are a few important details to keep in mind:.

In a recent development, now available Amazon ECS Gateway is available now in all commercial AWS Regions where ECS is available at no additional charge. You pay only for the underlying infrastructure provisioned in your account when services connect to a gateway, including applicable ALB charges, CloudWatch logs and metrics, ACM certificates, and data transfer charges. To learn more, visit the Amazon ECS Pricing page.

To get started, create your first gateway today in the ECS console, and send feedback to AWS re:Post for ECS or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

#184137. Latest Update: AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available

📅 22 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1237 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Latest Update: AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available

📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1237 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities.
  • Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process.
  • In a recent development, continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Today, we’re announcing the general availability of AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities. AWS Continuum is a security service that finds and validates code vulnerabilities, then delivers fixes as patches you can automate or as pull requests in your repositories. AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities confirms which findings are exploitable in your environment, ranks the resulting concerns by business impact, and proposes a fix for each one. Every remediation starts in a mode where Continuum proposes the fix and a person approves it before it ships. In the future, you will be able to decide which actions Continuum can take on its own, within the guardrails you define.

Using frontier artificial intelligence (AI) models, threat actors can turn a vulnerability disclosure into working exploit code in minutes, and the same tools that speed up development also increase the volume of findings your teams must process. If your organization runs a large application estate, your scanners likely produce thousands of findings a day, and many of them need no action. A finding can be unreachable, unexploitable, or already mitigated by a runtime control. Generic severity scores don’t tell you which resources a threat actor can actually reach, so a critical score on a dev-only utility looks the same as a medium score on a service one step away from a payments database. Previously, confirming whether a finding was exploitable took hours of manual investigation, and shipping a fix with confidence took days of coordination across security, infrastructure, and application teams, because the blast radius of a change is hard to assess without business context. To close that gap, Continuum proves which findings are exploitable and bounds the risk of each fix it proposes.

In a recent development, continuum builds a context graph from two primary sources: your code repositories and your AWS environment. For AWS, you set up a collector in the account and Region where your code runs. The collector gathers resource details such as AWS Config resources and network configuration so Continuum can judge whether a vulnerability is reachable over the network and what a threat actor could reach from it. From this graph, Continuum learns which systems are business-critical, who owns them, how services depend on one another, and which data each one touches. It uses that picture to identify your highest-value systems, such as customer data stores, payment pipelines, and authentication services, and then ranks each resulting issue by how close its attack path runs to those systems.

Continuum analyzes each finding against your code and its environment context and assigns an evidence level, such as a verdict proven by static analysis of the vulnerable code path. For findings it can reproduce, Continuum runs the exploit in an isolated sandbox and attaches proof-of-concept code with the reproduction steps. It produces the attack path, the supporting source analysis, and a blast radius assessment instead of a risk score alone. It also evaluates whether your existing defenses would detect and stop the validated path.

For each confirmed problem, Continuum generates a fix (a code patch, a dependency upgrade, or a configuration change) and opens it as a pull request in your connected repository, ready to review. Every fix requires human approval: you review and merge the pull request, so the final decision stays with your team. In the future, you will be able to build confidence in specific remediation classes and let Continuum apply those fixes automatically once its confidence gates pass, such as test coverage, scope bounds, and historical success rate.

According to recent reports, AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities in actionTo show how this works, I open AWS Continuum in the console and go to Code vulnerabilities. Before I can review issues, I set up an environment. I connect a code source, either a GitHub integration or an Amazon S3 bucket, and then create an environment that scans it on a schedule I choose. An Amazon S3 source has a couple of prerequisites: the bucket sits in the same account and AWS Region where I turn on AWS Continuum, and I grant access through an AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) role that AWS Continuum assumes. I can optionally add AWS infrastructure context by setting up an AWS Continuum collector in the account and Region where my code runs and authorizing my environment to use it. For the full requirements and steps, see the AWS Continuum User Guide.

The Overview page brings these pieces together in one place, showing my Code integrations, the Environments built on them, and the status of any AWS collector that supplies AWS resource context.

I open one of my environments. The Concerns tab lists validated, prioritized issues rather than raw scanner output, each with a severity, a status, and the time it was created. I choose one of the issues.

The Overview rates it High severity, with the status Completed and the remediation already Delivered to GitHub. The Risk assessment explains why. Continuum rates its Exploitability as Exploitable, with an evidence level of Static proven and a validation run status of Completed. Likelihood is High, since the service is reachable from an attacker, requires no authentication, and needs no user interaction. Impact is Moderate, which means an attacker gains the ability to modify business data, with a blast radius reaching other customers in the same tenant. A Proof section includes the source analysis behind the verdict.

Recent findings suggest that the Remediation section shows a fix already delivered as a pull request in GitHub, changing four files, with 50 lines added and 24 removed across the cart service. Continuum opens the fix as a pull request titled Continuum fix, and I choose View pull request to open it in GitHub. The console is explicit that a generated patch does not mean the matter is fixed. I still review and merge it, which keeps the final decision with my team. A Contributing findings section lists the specific scanner finding this issue was built from.

The pull request description carries the same risk assessment, remediation summary, and proof from the console, so whoever reviews it in GitHub sees the evidence without leaving their workflow.

The Findings tab lists the raw scanner findings across the environment, the evidence that problems are built from.

Recent findings suggest that the Scans tab shows the history of each scan with its status, origin, and request and completion times, and I use Configure scan frequency to change the cadence or Queue scan to run one on demand. The Configuration tab is where I manage the environment: the code and context sources it reads from, its code integrations, environment settings such as whether Continuum creates remediation patches, and the AWS collectors it uses for AWS context.

In a single workflow, I work through the validated problems in priority order with each scan, reviewing the evidence and scope behind each one before I approve and merge the fixes I trust. Every fix waits for my approval, so the backlog keeps shrinking while my team keeps control of what ships.

To learn more, visit the AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities product page and the User Guide. Give it a try in the AWS Continuum console today, and send us feedback through your usual AWS Support contacts.

Distributed LLM Training Across Metros: Streaming DiLoCo in MaxText

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (572 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Googleblog

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients.
  • In a recent development, to scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters.
  • According to recent reports, to address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Traditionally, training state-of-the-art Large Language Models (LLMs) relies on a monolithic cluster of accelerators, where all devices are collocated and tightly coupled via high-bandwidth to constantly synchronize gradients. However, physical and cost constraints make scaling a single slice increasingly difficult.

In a recent development, to scale further, we can connect multiple compute slices across geographically distributed datacenters. However, when training across multiple datacenters over wide-area networks (WAN), standard data-parallel training suffers from severe network stalls because slow WAN transfers cannot be fully overlapped with computation.

According to recent reports, to address this, the Google DeepMind and Google Research teams developed DiLoCo (Distributed Low-Communication), a distributed optimization algorithm designed to make training resilient to these low-bandwidth, high-latency connections. In this blog post, we discuss the core concepts of DiLoCo, how it is implemented in MaxText (Google's open-source JAX-based LLM training framework), and the performance benefits it brings to large-scale LLM training on Google Cloud.

DiLoCo was introduced by Google DeepMind in the paper DiLoCo: Distributed Low-Communication Training of Language Models. Instead of synchronizing gradients across all devices at every single training step (as in standard Data Parallelism), DiLoCo partitions training across M independent compute groups, referred to as learners, and allows each learner to perform many local optimization steps independently before communicating across groups.

Despite communicating significantly less frequently (by a factor of H, e.g., 1-2 orders of magnitude less) than standard synchronous training, DiLoCo has been shown to achieve comparable convergence and model quality.

Industry observers note that the Vanilla DiLoCo described above reduces total communication volume by a factor of H, however, all learners still transmit their weight deltas for the entire model all at once at every H-th step. On a thin network pipe, that full-model transfer creates a large periodic stall every H steps. This glitch is alleviated by Streaming DiLoCo, which is described in the next section.

In multi-slice training, communication within a single slice is handled by high-speed Inter-Chip Interconnects (ICI). When scaling to multiple slices, synchronization across slices must traverse the Data Center Network (DCN) or, if the slices are geographically distributed, wide-area networks (WAN).

Industry observers note that within a single datacenter, DCN bandwidth is high enough that JAX and XLA can often hide standard Data Parallel all-reduce collectives by overlapping gradient communication with backward-pass computation. Across datacenters or congested links, however, bandwidth drops and latency rises sharply. Standard DP stalls at every step waiting for global gradient synchronization, collapsing Model FLOPS Utilization (MFU).

Streaming DiLoCo eliminates this synchronization stall by partitioning the model's parameters into P disjoint fragments. Over the course of H steps, every single fragment in the model is synchronized exactly once, achieving the exact same outer-loop cadence as vanilla DiLoCo without spiky bandwidth utilization.

Using a roofline model (similar to the JAX Scaling Book), we can calculate the network bandwidth required to prevent communication stalls for a model with ∣Θ∣ parameters (at b bytes per parameter, e.g., b=2 for bfloat16) and per-step compute time tstep=tfwd+tbwd. For example, the standard Data Parallel algorithm transfers 2∣Θ∣b bytes per sync via an all-reduce collective, which is a distributed reduce-scatter where each node reduces a different part, followed by an all-gather so all participants receive all parts. To achieve zero communication stalls, we overlap the reduce-scatter of the gradients with the backward pass, which produces them and takes tbwd time. Therefore, the peak required bandwidth is Bdp ≈ 2∣Θ∣b / tbwd.

#184134. Swapping Jolt's sorted collections to a B+tree

📅 23 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 9m • 📚 Deep Dive (1792 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Yogthos ↗ Open Full Page

Swapping Jolt's sorted collections to a B+tree

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1792 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Yogthos

⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Until recently, sorted-map and sorted-set in Jolt were a straight port of Clojure's PersistentTreeMap, which is backed by a persistent red-black tree.
  • Sources indicate that so, naturally I got curious to see if a different data structure could be used for the same job which might have a lower overhead.
  • Sources indicate that each red-black node in Jolt was a five-slot Scheme vector holding a color along with the key, the value, and its two children.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Until recently, sorted-map and sorted-set in Jolt were a straight port of Clojure's PersistentTreeMap, which is backed by a persistent red-black tree. Using a red-black tree has worked well for Clojure, and it provides a solid foundation for backing these data structures. However, red-black trees have a downside, which is that every entry gets its own small node, meaning that every step of a lookup follows a pointer to a different place in memory.

Sources indicate that so, naturally I got curious to see if a different data structure could be used for the same job which might have a lower overhead. Turns out that a red-black tree can indeed be swapped out for a B+tree here. Updating Jolt's sorted collections along with the java.util.TreeMap and TreeSet shims to use a persistent B+tree dropped peak memory by 40% while making most operations faster at every size, as we'll see later in the benchmarks.

Sources indicate that each red-black node in Jolt was a five-slot Scheme vector holding a color along with the key, the value, and its two children. And all that translates into 48 bytes of metadata per entry on top of the key and value themselves. A map with 4 million entries needs a tree around 22 levels deep, so, a lookup can end up visiting about 22 nodes scattered across the heap. And once the tree outgrows the CPU cache, each of these visits is likely to be a cache miss as well.

As you might've guessed, writes also have a similar problem. Since a persistent tree can't modify a node in place, an assoc has to copy every node on the path from the root to the change, which results in 22 small allocations followed by rebalancing at that size.

The key advantage of using a B+tree is that it keeps data in leaves of up to 16 entries and branches through inner nodes of up to 32 children with each node being a single Scheme vector. In this layout, a leaf is written as #(#t k0 v0 k1 v1 ...) with keys and values sitting side by side in one contiguous block. An inner node also stores the largest key below it right next to each child.

According to recent reports, now, the same tree of 4 million entries becomes just 5 levels deep instead of 22. On top of that, a lookup within each node has to only search through adjacent slots that are already in cache. Writes still have to copy the path from the root, but that's now a quarter of the work with each one being copied as a block.

Unsurprisingly, memory use improved significantly, since a full leaf holds 16 entries in 34 machine words, needing only 17 bytes per entry against the red-black tree's 48. Nodes are also allowed to drop to half before they merge, so 34 bytes per entry ends up being the worst case here. It would be ideal to keep the common case near full as much as possible, and a trick that can be used here is to start a fresh node when append goes past either end of the tree rather than splitting a full node into two half-empty ones. A common case for this would be building from ascending keys, which ends up packing every node using this approach. Similarly, deletes end up borrowing entries from a neighbour or merging with it to keep the tree balanced without needing rotations.

Of course, nothing in life is free, and B+trees do have a weakness of their own. While they're much faster for large collections, building small ones of tens to hundreds of entries one insert at a time ended up being around 15% slower than the red-black tree. The reason goes back to the respective structure of each data structure. Once a map has 17 entries, that requires a root with two leaves, and every insert needs to copy the whole path. So, at smaller sizes the B+tree has to move more bytes per insert than the red-black tree, which is the trade-off.

Sources indicate that luckily, there is a way around the problem by changing how collections get built. We can first collect the inputs for into, the sorted-map and sorted-set constructors, and multi-argument conj/assoc to check whether they're already in order, then skip the sort if they are. Additionally, we can drop duplicate keys by keeping the first key along with the last value, which allows us to bulk-load the leaves. The batches can now get merged with the collection that already has entries. Meanwhile, small sources of 8 or fewer entries that go into an empty collection continue to use plain conj, because the overhead of buffering would end up costing more than it actually saves. With these changes in place, the worst remaining case ends up being a 4 entry map at 1.05x, which is effectively as good as a red-black tree.

So, now that we've discussed how B+trees work, and what makes them a good alternative to red-black trees in this scenario, let's look at some actual benchmark numbers comparing the two approaches. The numbers were measured using optimized binaries across several runs on an M1 Max with 64 GB. The JVM comparisons use Clojure 1.12.6 on OpenJDK 20. A ratio under 1.0 means the B+tree is faster.

Times are for the whole operation over the collection, which includes building it, doing a lookup for every key, removing every key, and replacing every value. Keys are also scrambled to avoid a degenerate sequential case.

As we can see, lookups win at every size, by 23 to 33%. Builds and writes stay flat below 64 entries. Notably, even a 4 entry map ends up being a single leaf searched in place, meaning that it doesn't pay for the extra machinery.

It has been revealed that the reduce-kv result stands out because it's a result of a fix in the fresh layout. The original red-black tree code built a map entry for every pair going through the generic sequence path. Walking the leaves and passing each key/value pair straight to the function avoids having to allocate memory for each slot. And since the B+tree can seek to a key to start reading from that leaf without having to rebuild a stack of nodes from the root on every call, repeatedly taking the first element of a subseq gets faster as well.

From here on out we hit a cliff where the cache matters more than anything else.

According to recent reports, while performance looked good for thousands of elements, it was also key to check what would happen with collections having millions of entries in order to make sure nothing broke or regressed badly at this scale. The following benchmark builds a sorted map and a sorted set from scrambled keys and then runs a mix of operations over them.

Recent findings suggest that and the good news is that every operation at this scale is also faster than the previous version. Not only that, but Jolt is now faster than the JVM at building sets, walking, reducing, and range queries, while the two are roughly even on contains? and the map build. Finally, point lookups and deletes are still about 1.5x slower than the JVM, which uses a red-black tree backed PersistentTreeMap thanks to the magic of the highly optimized JIT that the JVM enjoys.

Recent findings suggest that peak resident memory for the 4M run nearly halved, going from 1.73 GB to 1.04 GB with the B+tree. It's worth noting that the process holds a 4M entry map with its 4M entry set, along with the garbage from building them. So, the numbers here reflect the whole program rather than just the trees themselves. And the JVM run peaked at 4 to 6 GB, but that's mostly an artifact of how the JVM collects garbage with its default settings, so we shouldn't read too much into that.

Industry observers note that you might have noticed that the scrambled builds slow down sharply somewhere between 1M and 2M entries. The JVM also shows the same jump with its sort going from 16 to 93 ms. In both cases, the cause is that the working set ends up falling out of cache, making lookup more expensive.

As I mentioned earlier, Jolt's TreeMap and TreeSet shims are built on the sorted map. These were implemented using a naive approach where they went through it one generic operation at a time. Each put looked up the key and then inserted it, having to walk the tree twice, while navigation methods like floorKey built a subseq and took its first element.

Sources indicate that now, all of these operations have been updated to use the tree directly, meaning that a put or remove is one walk, while operations like floorKey are a single seek. The size of a bounded view can now be computed by adding up whole leaves and only scanning the two partial leaves at the edges. Times are for 20,000 operations.

That's 4 to 70 times faster than the original version, with headMap size beating the JVM, which needs to walk the view in order to count it. But the writes are still about 4x the JVM, and can't be closed with this design because the Java mutates its nodes in place, while Jolt's TreeMap is a mutable wrapper around a persistent tree. So, there's no way around each put having to copy about five nodes.

According to recent reports, iteration order, which key is kept on a duplicate, which value wins, the argument order passed to custom comparators, and returning the identical collection from a no-op assoc all work as they did before. But there is one thing that's different from the JVM, which stems from the layout of the trees. Building a 1,024 entry map from ascending keys now calls the comparator 1,023 times while the JVM's red-black tree calls it 12,301 times. So, code that counts comparator calls will see different numbers on Jolt.

It has been revealed that what this exercise reveals is the importance of the memory layout used by the backing data structure. All the operations do the same logical work as before, but they now have to touch about a fifth as many nodes with the data inside each node being contiguous.

Switching to use a B+tree was not a free win, though, since it required a separate batch build path to make the switch efficient for code that builds lots of medium-sized maps, which adds some complexity to the implementation. If you're making a similar kind of optimization, always be sure to measure the middle sizes along with the extremes.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo.
  • Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo.
  • The rest of the week had a sharper edge.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that A few weeks ago I presented to a small group of commercial and technology leaders from Brazilian agribusiness at the AWS office in São Paulo. My talk ran through where generative AI fits across the different stages of an agribusiness operation, and the point I kept returning to is that the markets we call traditional are exactly the ones where keeping up with this technology decides who ends up ahead of the curve. Nobody there was arguing about whether AI belongs in agriculture. The questions were about delivery: who receives the output, in which language, on which device, often while driving between farms. That is why a launch I might otherwise have filed under routine leads my list this week. The Amazon Polly Generative engine upgrade added 14 latest voices, two of them in Brazilian Portuguese. When your user has both hands on a steering wheel, the interface is a voice.

Presenting “GenAI no Agronegócio Brasileiro” at the AWS office in São Paulo.

The rest of the week had a sharper edge. The biggest launch is a security service built on the premise that the gap between a vulnerability being disclosed and a vulnerability being exploited has effectively closed, and AWS published the honeypot evidence for exactly that in the same week. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

Industry observers note that AWS Continuum for code vulnerabilities is now generally available AWS Continuum reframes vulnerability management as an end-to-end job rather than a scanner that hands you a list. It builds a context graph from your repositories and your AWS environment, assigns each finding an evidence level, and reproduces exploitable findings in an isolated sandbox with proof-of-concept code so you see the concern rather than a severity label. It ranks complications by how close the attack path runs to business-critical systems, then opens the fix as a pull request. The control boundary matters: every remediation right now requires human approval, so you review and merge the pull request, with autonomous classes of fix gated behind confidence thresholds for the future.

The “why now” came from AWS’s own honeypots in the same week. Amazon Threat Intelligence found a PHP2Shell exploitation attempt in MadPot telemetry dated October 17, four days before CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619 were publicly disclosed, and on disclosure day proof-of-concept exploits were circulating around 02:00 UTC, roughly twelve hours before the embargo was due to lift at 14:00 UTC. The practical reading is direct: a patch window measured in days assumes a delay that no longer exists, and an investigation should start from the earliest known exploitation rather than from the disclosure date. AWS also published the AWS WAF mitigations for the same CVEs. Continuum is available in US East (N. Virginia) and US West (Oregon).

Recent findings suggest that introducing Amazon ECS Gateway Amazon ECS Gateway splits the work of exposing a service between the people who own the network and the people who own the application. Platform teams define one gateway with the organization’s subnets, security groups, TLS certificates, listener settings, and AWS WAF web ACLs. Application teams opt in by adding a gateway connector to the service definition, and ECS gives them an ACM certificate, a unique DNS hostname, listener rules, a target group, and a security group that admits traffic only from the Application Load Balancer.

It has been revealed that the numbers make the economics clear: up to 25 services share a single ALB, ECS provisions the first ALB on first connect and removes ALBs when they are no longer needed, and a gateway can associate with up to 10,000 clusters, with five gateways per cluster. You can adopt it incrementally with UpdateService while your existing load balancer stays in place. Amazon ECS Gateway is available in all commercial Regions where Amazon ECS is available, at no additional charge.

Last week’s debuts Here are some launches that caught my attention this week.

Recent findings suggest that amazon Polly delivers a major upgrade to its Generative engine – The Generative engine now runs a larger, more expressive catalog: 57 generative voices across 11 languages and 25 locales, with 14 newly introduced voices across 9 locales and Hindi and Finnish generally available for the first time. Two of the new voices are Brazilian Portuguese, Leo and Carolina. It is a drop-in upgrade, so the voice names, the same SynthesizeSpeech call, and the price all stay the same while the output gets more natural.

Industry observers note that AWS introduces TorchNeuron: native PyTorch support for AWS Trainium (public beta) – TorchNeuron is an open source PyTorch backend that lets you run your model on Trainium by switching to .to(‘neuron’), a configuration change instead of a rewrite, with eager execution and torch.compile intact. It integrates with the Neuron Kernel Interface for custom operators, and it works on Trainium2 and Trainium3 instances. If you want the bigger picture on why hardware choice should not lock in your software, the AWS Insights piece on that theme is a good companion read, and the release lands alongside AWS Neuron 2.33.

Upcoming ways to customize models with Amazon SageMaker AI, without managing GPUs – Training sessions are now generally available, giving you control of the post-training loop, including custom loss functions and reward signals, while SageMaker AI handles GPU allocation, distributed execution, fault recovery, and checkpoint storage. You pay for the tokens SageMaker AI processes, and the meter stops while your reward function scores a batch. There is a full technical walkthrough, the training session APIs, and new support for Muse Glimmer, Qwen 3.8, and Ministral 3.

It has been revealed that structured outputs for Claude models available on Amazon Bedrock – You can now get schema-compliant JSON back from any Anthropic Claude model on Amazon Bedrock, across both the bedrock-runtime and bedrock-mantle endpoints, without custom parsing, retry logic, or post-processing. That makes jobs like pulling every required field from a financial report, parsing clinical notes, or routing support tickets by intent far more reliable to automate.

According to recent reports, amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey now supports online migration with zero downtime – You can migrate self-managed Valkey or Redis OSS on Amazon EC2 into ElastiCache Serverless with zero downtime, meaning zero errors returned to the client during the move, measured the way the ElastiCache SLA measures availability. You prepare the migration, start the data sync, then choose a manual or automatic cutover, with no third-party replication tools. It is available in all commercial Regions, the China Regions, and the AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

Other AWS news Here are some additional projects and posts that you might find interesting.

Recent findings suggest that discover tools at runtime with AWS Agent Registry – AWS Agent Registry is a managed catalog for MCP servers, agents, and agent skills, so an orchestrator can search approved capabilities at runtime instead of compiling every tool in at build time. This walkthrough shows the discover, instantiate, and execute loop in a working sample, with search results that return connection metadata but never invocation credentials.

Recent findings suggest that tokenomics for coding agents: benchmark cost and quality on your own code – Coding assistants replay a growing transcript on every turn, so their cost math is nothing like ordinary inference. This post gives you open source tooling to measure model, harness, and hosting choices on your own repositories and build a cost-and-quality frontier you own, with sample results where routing came out 44.7 percent cheaper for 4.8 percent lower mean quality.

Sources indicate that how U.S. Bank migrated 119 TB from Oracle Exadata to Amazon RDS for Oracle – U.S. Bank moved four Oracle Exadata databases totaling about 119 TB to Amazon RDS for Oracle using a config-driven pipeline built on Oracle XTTS, AWS DataSync, and Amazon EFS. The initial baseline copy finished in about 7 days with zero data loss and cutovers averaging roughly four hours per database, over a bandwidth-capped Direct Connect link.

Upcoming AWS events Mark your calendars for these upcoming events.

Recent findings suggest that AWS re:Invent – AWS re:Invent runs November 30 to December 4 in Las Vegas, with more than 2,200 sessions. The session catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so now is the time to build your schedule.

AWS Community Days – AWS Community Day Brasil Norte takes place in Belém on October 31, closing out the 2026 Brazilian community season. Check the hub for events near you.

In a recent development, that’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!
