AWS Weekly Roundup: GPT-6.1 Terra on Bedrock, Step Functions as agent tools, and more (November 2, 2026)

📅 02 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1418 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The agentic releases that stayed with me last week had nothing to do with how capable a model is.
  • OpenAI’s newest Terra model reached Amazon Bedrock priced well below the model beside it, and two post-quantum releases landed for a deadline nobody can put on a calendar yet.
  • It has been revealed that headlinesOpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock, and what interests me is where it sits rather than what it tops.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The agentic releases that stayed with me last week had nothing to do with how capable a model is. They were about reach. AWS Step Functions, which already orchestrates over 220 AWS services, can now be handed to an agent as a tool, so workflows teams already trust became callable without a rewrite. In the same week, the AI blog published how one engagement platform exposed roughly 400 internal API operations the same way. Neither story involves rebuilding anything, only describing what exists and letting the agent find it.

The other thread was cost. OpenAI’s newest Terra model reached Amazon Bedrock priced well below the model beside it, and two post-quantum releases landed for a deadline nobody can put on a calendar yet. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

It has been revealed that headlinesOpenAI GPT-6.1 Terra is now generally available on Amazon Bedrock, and what interests me is where it sits rather than what it tops. Terra is the everyday-workload line of the GPT-6 family. In OpenAI’s Agents’ Last Exam evaluation it scored 15 percentage points higher than GPT-5.6 Terra, performed on par with GPT-6 Astra, and completed tasks more than three times faster than both. Those are OpenAI’s figures, not an independent test. The price is what I would check first: input and output tokens are at least 50% lower than GPT-6.1 Sol and GPT-5.6 Terra. It takes up to 1 million input tokens with text and image input, and you can reach it from the Bedrock APIs or ChatGPT Work and Codex.

AWS Step Functions workflows are now available as AI agent tools through Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Gateway, which connects agents to tools over the Model Context Protocol (MCP). The division of labor is the idea: the agent decides when to run a workflow and what input to pass; Step Functions runs each step exactly as you defined it. A support agent can trigger a refund, and the eligibility check, the manager approval, and the credit still happen in that order every time, because the ordering was never the model’s to improvise. Your existing Standard and Express workflows qualify as connector targets, and agents can also look up runs. It’s available in all Regions where AgentCore Gateway is, at standard rates.

Last week’s releases Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:.

AWS Key Management Service now supports ML-KEM for post-quantum key encapsulation – You can now establish a shared secret with a post-quantum algorithm using AWS KMS keys, with private keys in FIPS 140-3 Level 3 validated HSMs. All three NIST FIPS 203 parameter sets are supported through Encapsulate, which produces a random 32-byte shared secret and its ciphertext, and Decapsulate, which recovers it. The threat is harvest now, decrypt later: an adversary records today’s key exchange and recovers the secret once quantum computers are powerful enough. It’s available everywhere KMS runs except the Middle East (UAE and Bahrain) and China Regions. Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL added post-quantum TLS key exchange the same week, on versions 18 and higher.

AWS IAM Identity Center now supports cross-Region trusted identity propagation – You can now carry a user’s identity with their request to AWS services in another Region. This removes a genuine architectural constraint: trusted identity propagation used to require every service accessing that identity to sit in the same Region, which left two unappealing options, broad IAM roles that cannot distinguish individual customers, or consolidating all your services into a single Region. Now the identity travels with the request automatically, so you grant access by user and group membership and audit who accessed what. It’s available at no additional cost everywhere IAM Identity Center runs.

Sources indicate that amazon ECS now supports GPU sharing with NVIDIA Multi-Process Service (MPS) – You can now run multiple Amazon ECS tasks concurrently on a single NVIDIA GPU, the practical answer to work that only ever uses a fraction of one, like small-model inference and multi-model serving. You declare the GPU memory each container needs and can optionally cap its share of GPU compute, and ECS places tasks on GPUs with available capacity as your services scale, with no code changes. It works on ECS Managed Instances and ECS on Amazon EC2, and on Managed Instances it watches the MPS control daemon and replaces the instance if it turns unhealthy. It’s available in all commercial and AWS GovCloud (US) Regions.

It has been revealed that AWS Lambda supports Seekable OCI (SOCI) lazy loading for Lambda Managed Instances – You can now have AWS Lambda fetch only the files needed at each stage of startup instead of pulling a whole container image first, which AWS puts at up to 70% off container startup time. You create a SOCI index, push it to Amazon ECR, point the image URI at the indexed tag, and Lambda detects it automatically. The technique also reached Amazon SageMaker AI training and processing jobs, with benchmarks: lazy loading held at 3 to 11 seconds regardless of image size, against a median 3 minutes 42 seconds for a 13.2 GB image, a range they report as 8x to 46x.

Amazon EKS Auto Mode now supports Kubernetes Gateway API – You can now declare how traffic reaches your applications with Gateway and HTTPRoute resources on Amazon EKS without installing a separate controller, and EKS Auto Mode provisions and manages the underlying AWS load balancing infrastructure. You get HTTP and gRPC routing, cross-namespace routing, weighted traffic splitting, header-based routing, and automatic TLS certificate discovery through AWS Certificate Manager. Existing Ingress workloads keep working alongside them, so this is additive rather than a migration. Gateway API support is included with EKS Auto Mode; standard load balancing charges apply.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s New with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:.

How Nubank automated disaster recovery with the AWS DevOps Agent – Nubank serves more than 140 million customers across Brazil, Mexico, and Colombia, and classifies over 300 business flows as critical, each tested on a regulator’s schedule. Nubank reports that handing evidence collection and report writing to the AWS DevOps Agent cut a test cycle from about 4.3 hours to roughly 40 minutes, and quadrupled flow coverage in 2026 to more than 160. One execution terminated more than 900 EKS instances under synthetic traffic with AWS Fault Injection Service, producing the evidence its regulator needed.

Industry observers note that how MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway – Roughly 400 internal REST API operations, built by 25 teams, sitting in private VPCs across seven Regions, with tenant identity that could never become a parameter the model gets to set. MoEngage estimates the managed path saved about six months of platform engineering. The detail worth stealing: a full tool listing would have crossed 20,000 tokens per connection, so agents search for tools by describing a task instead of receiving the catalog.

Reducing petabyte-scale S3 storage costs with evidence-based lifecycle rules – The hard part isn’t deciding to act, it’s knowing which data has gone cold and where it can safely live. This uses S3 Storage Lens groups and Storage Class Analysis to prove access patterns before moving anything. In the engagement described, 5.8 PB of logs in Amazon S3 Standard at approximately $241,000 per month highlighted an access ratio below 0.1% past 90 days, and a 90-day transition to Glacier Instant Retrieval cut the bill by roughly 70%, a figure the author ties to that workload.

Sources indicate that AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4, with more than 2,200 sessions. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up.

AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders. The 2026 season is winding down as re:Invent approaches, so check the hub for what’s still on.

It has been revealed that join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

That’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

Nightmare mode: simulating disk failures

📅 24 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 17 min read (3402 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Antithesis

⏱️ ~17 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • November 24, 2026 | Anjana Ratnayake, Forward deployed engineer | Teymour Aldridge, Forward deployed engineer.
  • It has been revealed that building a correct distributed system is really, really hard.
  • Many of our customers build systems where storing data reliably is paramount.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

November 24, 2026 | Anjana Ratnayake, Forward deployed engineer | Teymour Aldridge, Forward deployed engineer.

It has been revealed that building a correct distributed system is really, really hard. Building a correct distributed system that has to store data and never lose it is even harder.

Many of our customers build systems where storing data reliably is paramount. Storage is hard even when nothing goes wrong. For example, some customers watch how full their disks are and compact data when necessary to reclaim space, and shard it across machines before any one disk hits its limits. Some maintain a write-ahead log so they can recover from a process restart. Others rely on a careful sequence of operations to guarantee durability and atomicity, for example writing a new copy of a file and renaming it over the old one, so that a change happens completely or not at all.

Unfortunately, storage devices are unreliable, which only adds further complexity to every interaction with the disk. Consider a single write. If it fails with an error, the system has to decide whether it is safe to retry or whether it has to give up. If it fails because the disk is out of space, the system may have to trigger compaction before it can continue. Even creating a file can fail because the filesystem has run out of inodes, and the system then has to delete other files to make room.

It has been revealed that moreover, unreliability can come in the form of latency. A disk can be slow, for example because of I/O contention or a failing device, which can then stretch operations out so they overlap in ways they normally wouldnât. If a read and a write end up happening at the same time, the reader may see the old data, the fresh data, or a random interleaving of the two.

Recent findings suggest that complexity also arises once you assume the disk will not always be there. If a write succeeds and the machine loses power immediately afterwards, a read after the restart could see all of the data, a random part of it, or none of it.

Recent findings suggest that on the Antithesis Forward Deployed Engineering team, weâve had recurring discussions with customers who build this critical software, and who would like to inject disk faults or storage errors during their Antithesis simulations to mimic these kinds of situations and to ensure their software can handle it. One of the first things we realized is that different customers had vastly different expectations of their storage, and of the guarantees it should provide. This was further complicated by some running on the ext4 filesystem, and some on XFS or ZFS, each with its own behaviors under failure.

This diversity of requirements has made it hard to build a one-size-fits-all solution up front. Instead, we worked with individual customers to build several solutions, geared to their specific use cases. For instance, to test space reclamation logic weâd simulate filling up the whole filesystem.

Other approaches include shouting at the disks.

According to recent reports, once weâd got a sense of the requirements of different customers, we worked to incorporate these pieces of the puzzle into a comprehensive filesystem fault injection mechanism. In this post, weâll give a tour of the disk faults that a ânightmare modeâ fault injector needs to be able to emulate. Weâll start with the fault everyone asks for first, power failure, and explain what it took to emulate it convincingly. From there weâll get into the subtler things a disk can do: torn writes, I/O errors (including the one behind the fsyncgate bug), and the latency faults that shake out concurrency bugs.

Before we get into faults, weâll give some background on how file writes work in the âhappy pathâ case.

When a program writes to a file, the data does not go to disk right away. Instead, it goes into the kernelâs page cache. The kernel then writes it to disk on its own schedule, through a process called writeback. If a program needs the data on disk immediately, it can call fsync, which tells the kernel to write that fileâs data to disk and doesnât return until the write has finished. Data that is written but not fsynced could be destroyed by a power loss.

The diagram below indicates these steps for a successful write to disk:.

It has been revealed that now letâs start looking at what happens when things go wrong. We started with power loss because it seemed like the fault most of our customers would care about.

Antithesis already has a related fault type, node kills, which randomly SIGKILL a container. The SIGKILL destroys the process, but has no effect on the machine, which keeps running, so the kernel and its page cache carry on as if nothing happened. Every write the process completed still makes its way to disk, fsync or no fsync, courtesy of the kernelâs writeback mechanism. As far as the process is concerned, a SIGKILL is a fairly polite way to die, since you only lose data that the process never handed to the kernel.

The diagram below reveals how data that was written but never fsynced survives the SIGKILL and lands on disk anyway:.

Sources indicate that A power failure is less polite. It loses everything the kernel accepted but hadnât synced yet. Data that has been written but not yet fsynced is simply gone:.

Recent findings suggest that unfortunately, when weâre simulating faults in Antithesis, we canât just pull the plug on the machine. So the next best option was to fake it. That meant dealing with the two things that stop a container kill from causing data or cache loss: the kernelâs page cache, which holds on to unsynced data, and the kernelâs writeback, which saves unsynced data to disk.

The problem was that both of these live inside the kernel, out of our reach. Currently, there is no way to ask the kernel to forget whatâs in its cache, or to stop the kernelâs automatic writeback. However, we found a way around this: LazyFS, an open-source filesystem from INESC TEC and Jepsen.

LazyFS uses FUSE, a Linux feature that lets a userspace program act as a filesystem. Because every read and write goes through LazyFS, it can hold written data in its own internal cache, emulating the kernelâs page cache in user space. Writes to LazyFS stay in the internal cache until the program calls fsync, and only then does LazyFS write it to persistent storage. Also, there is no background writeback to save it in the meantime. This gives us the ability to âforgetâ unsynced data at any convenient moment, simply by clearing the cache. If we do that at the same moment we kill the application, the two together are indistinguishable from a real power loss.

Hereâs a diagram of we can use LazyFS to emulate power loss:.

Sources indicate that before settling on FUSE, we looked at a couple of other mechanisms for injecting faults. eBPF was tempting, since it makes some faults, like returning a particular error code from a syscall, easy to implement. However, it would be difficult to emulate power failure, since it only allows us to watch and tweak calls as they go by. It canât hold on to data and release it (or lose it) later, which is the trick we needed. We also thought about using a custom block device, but that had the opposite problem: it can hold data, but it sits at the wrong level of abstraction. Since itâs below the filesystem, it sees blocks rather than syscalls, which makes syscall-level faults hard to implement. Power loss is especially tricky because you canât tell data that arrived through an fsync from data the kernelâs writeback happened to push out. That would cost us the strictness that catches missing fsyncs.

So LazyFS was very useful to us, and we want to extend a thank you to the authors for writing such a high quality tool. We ran a patched version (extended with additional fault types) for a while on a number of customer tenants, and it found some subtle data loss bugs.

It has been revealed that after that, we decided to implement our own FUSE filesystem: Amnesia. We wanted to move to Rust for its memory safety, and to rework the design so the model was simpler and faster, since we planned to build a lot more on top of it.

For instance, Amnesia works directly on inodes, whereas LazyFS uses the path for every operation and has to map it back to the inode. Since a path is only a name for a file, this makes operations like renames, hard links, and deleting a file that is still open awkward to track. Working with inodes instead makes that complexity disappear. Amnesia also never touches a real disk. LazyFS writes synced data through to the backing filesystem. Amnesia keeps both the volatile state and the âdurableâ state in memory, which allows us to model an fsync as a bookkeeping update instead of another real I/O. This makes it much faster, and just as safe, because the machine never actually loses power. We made a number of other changes too, which we will get into below.

Beyond the design, LazyFS introduced us to the subtler effects of a real power loss: torn writes and torn sequences of writes, both caused by the fact that the kernel and the disk do not persist data in the order or the units a program might expect.

The LazyFS paper by Ramos et al. is a good read if you want the details.

It also made us aware of the wrinkles of working at the FUSE layer. For instance, the kernel page cache still sits in front of the FUSE filesystem, and it can be holding copies of the data we just âlostâ by emulating a power failure. Thankfully, LazyFS had already worked out the right FUSE settings and patterns to make sure the program never sees them.

Building on FUSE made it easy to add disk I/O errors, another fault type that our customers wanted. The obvious approach is to simply return the error, and that model alone was enough to find some bugs. But because we emulate the kernel page cache, we can sometimes apply the possible side effects of these errors to it, which gives us a higher degree of fidelity.

Sources indicate that out of the box, LazyFS does not simulate disk I/O errors as a form of fault injection, so this was new ground for us. We added the ability to return a few disk I/O error types on syscalls. One of the most interesting ones was EIO (âError: Input/Outputâ, the generic âdisk failedâ error) on fsync.

Recent findings suggest that this error can interact with the kernel page cache in surprising ways. This is exactly whatâs behind the infamous fsyncgate bug. The discovery led to PostgreSQL fixing how it handles a failed fsync (it now crashes and recovers from its log rather than trying again), and it changed how the rest of us read fsyncâs promise for good. As Craig Ringer, the PostgreSQL developer who reported the problem, put it:.

When fsync() returns success it means âall writes since the last fsync have hit diskâ but we assume it means âall writes since the last SUCCESSFUL fsync have hit diskâ.

To understand why Craig is correct, we need some background on what happens during an fsync on a typical Linux filesystem such as ext4. The kernelâs page cache holds file data in fixed-size chunks called pages, and marks a page as âdirtyâ when it has been changed but not yet written to disk. When a program calls fsync, the kernel sends each of the fileâs dirty pages to the storage device through a driver. Crucially, the kernel clears a pageâs dirty flag before handing it off. The fsync then waits for the driver to report whether each write succeeded.

Now suppose one of those writes to the device fails. The fsync will then return EIO, but nothing goes back and marks the page dirty again. As far as the kernel is concerned, that page is now clean, so neither the next fsync nor the background writeback will ever try to submit it to the device again. Since there are no dirty pages associated with the file, the next fsync succeeds. Unless the program happens to write the same data again and re-dirties the pages, that data never reaches the disk.

Industry observers note that we can emulate this scenario in the FUSE layer. When the fault fires, fsync returns EIO and the affected pages are marked clean in our internal cache, without being written to persistent storage. A retried fsync then succeeds, but the data will be lost at the next emulated power failure unless the program writes it again and calls fsync.

Building on FUSE also let us add âdisk latencyâ, another commonly requested fault type.

According to recent reports, disk latency is really about finding concurrency bugs. Talking to the disk can be slow and unpredictable, and programs that assume otherwise can have races. These races can occur for several reasons. For example, data may land on the disk in an unpredictable order, or land in the kernel page cache in pieces rather than all at once. So we wanted to make those races easier to find.

We currently support two kinds of latency fault:.

Completing operations out of order. Instead of answering syscalls in the order they arrive, we let the fuzzer decide the order they complete in.

It has been revealed that since Amnesia sits underneath the program and sees every operation as a request, it can decide whether to answer immediately or hold on to the request. For instance, when data from a write operation arrives, we sometimes hold onto it with a deadline while other operations continue to be processed (the deadline provides a backstop: once it passes, the operation finishes no matter what). The fuzzer then decides when the parked operation should be executed next.

Recent findings suggest that partially completed operations. Syscalls arenât atomic, and a read racing a write can see the write partially applied. Suppose a program overwrites a few kilobytes of a file while another thread reads the same range. On ext4 the reader can see the old contents, the new contents, or a patchwork of old and new chunks. We let the fuzzer pick which of those the reader gets.

We implemented this in Amnesia by holding a write and splitting it into small chunks. Instead of applying them all, we let the fuzzer decide which chunks are applied immediately and which are held back. Combined with the out-of-order completion above, this means a read that arrives while the write is parked will likely be answered from the partially applied state, so it sees the same mix of old and upcoming data that a real race could produce.

It has been revealed that similarly, reads can be held and split into pieces that are captured at different moments. For instance, a single read can return the start of the file from before a write and the end from after it. With several operations parked on the same file at once, the fuzzer picks the order they finish in. We ensure that every combination it tries is a legal interleaving that the kernel page cache or disk could have produced.

According to recent reports, we built our FUSE filesystem to work hand in hand with the Antithesis fault injector and fuzzer. This lets us inject power failures, torn writes and disk I/O errors at moments our fuzzer considers âinterestingâ. It also means disk faults are controlled the same way as our other faults, so we get the benefits of swarm testing along the way.

Sources indicate that unlike our normal node kills fault, which could be interesting at any moment, with power failures we only need to sample one moment from one of the three categories of moments where a power failure can land: before the syscall, during it, or after it. Consider a single disk operation. Within âbeforeâ or âafterâ, the exact timing doesnât matter: if power failure is emulated anywhere in that window it will lead to the same outcome. The interesting states that are uncovered âduringâ an operation are relatively short, so these moments are rare especially in systems that touch the disk infrequently. By tying the fault to the disk operation itself, we let the fuzzer spend less energy finding these vulnerable states and more energy exploring from them.

Industry observers note that our disk fault injector helps the fuzzer by decreasing the uninteresting state space it has to explore. Instead of letting the fuzzer cut the power at arbitrary instants, it makes the decision on each syscall and injects the fault from inside the FUSE filesystem.

Each time the program is in the middle of a disk operation, there are three specific points where the injector may fire a power failure: before any of the operation has been applied to the internal cache, after part of it has been applied, and after all of it has been applied (but before the syscall returns). These three points line up with the three categories above: nothing applied, partly applied, or fully applied. When it does fire a power failure, the FUSE filesystem kills the container, deletes the internal cache, and makes sure any active syscalls are handled correctly. We call these correlated faults, because the timing of each power failure is tied to a specific disk operation.

Sources indicate that our work on disk fault injection has already earned its keep by uncovering a number of bugs in customer software. One open-source bug that we can share is in bbolt, the storage engine behind etcd. We injected all the disk faults in this post while testing the system, but the relevant ones for this particular bug are power failure and error injection.

In a recent development, the concern comes from bbolt committing a transaction in two steps that are each followed by an fsync. First it writes the newly introduced data pages, then it writes a single meta page that points at them.

We found a case where the data pages are written successfully, but the fsync of the meta page fails with an EIO. That causes etcd to exit, which is fine.

On restart, bbolt reads the meta page back through the kernel page cache, where the unpersisted meta page still exists, and wrongly treats that transaction as committed. It rebuilds its free page list from that meta page, so the next commits can reuse pages that the on-disk meta page still points to.

Once the cached meta page is evicted, through our emulation of memory pressure or power loss, what remains on disk is an old meta page pointing at overwritten pages. From then on bbolt panics at every open. The etcd nodeâs write-ahead log canât help rebuild the store, because the node never gets past opening it.

This bug could only be found by an I/O error followed by a power failure, which is exactly the kind of problem our disk fault injection finds.

In a recent development, weâve covered a lot of ground: power failures, torn writes and torn sequences, disk I/O errors (including the one behind fsyncgate), and the latency faults that shake out concurrency bugs. All of these are available in our disk fault injector today, and the list keeps growing as customers tell us what keeps them up at night.

It has been revealed that our disk fault injector is customizable, so you donât have to turn everything on. You can start with the faults that worry you most â power loss for a storage engine, for example, or I/O errors â and add more over time.

If youâre an existing customer, ask your forward deployed engineer to deploy disk faults in your environment. If youâre not, and youâd like to see how your system holds up in nightmare mode, get in touch.

And if thereâs a disk failure youâve been bitten by that we havenât covered, weâd love to hear about it. The best faults in this post came from exactly those conversations :).

Quality IMAP, Part 2: Mailbox Concurrency

📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2566 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Deuxfleurs

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In the past year, we have been significantly improving the reliability and correctness of Aerogramme's IMAP implementation.
  • Aerogramme is an experimental email server (& calendar, contacts), designed to be geo-distributed, hosted outside of datacenters, on refurbished hardware, and reliable even in presence of network issues and hardware failures.
  • Recent findings suggest that this is the second post in a series in which we argue that implementing an IMAP server is not easy, essentially due to two classes of features that are fundamentally challenging to implement.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In the past year, we have been significantly improving the reliability and correctness of Aerogramme's IMAP implementation. This is the second part in a series discussing why implementing IMAP correctly is not so easy, and presenting our work on making Aerogramme's IMAP code as high-quality as we can. Today we focus on challenges that arise when considering concurrent access to a mailbox.

Aerogramme is an experimental email server (& calendar, contacts), designed to be geo-distributed, hosted outside of datacenters, on refurbished hardware, and reliable even in presence of network issues and hardware failures. It is built on top of Garage and shares the same philosophy. Aerogramme is AI-free: we do not wish to use unethical technology and prefer to spend effort on careful craftmanship and community-building.

Recent findings suggest that this is the second post in a series in which we argue that implementing an IMAP server is not easy, essentially due to two classes of features that are fundamentally challenging to implement. In the previous post, we talked about the first class of features: fine-grained retrieval and querying of email contents. In this post, we talk about the second class of features that make implementing an IMAP server tricky: concurrent access to user mailboxes.

Concurrent and distributed software are famously hard to get right; concurrency bugs are known to be hard to find. In our recent work on refining Aerogramme we have tried to approach the problem from different angles. This is the topic of this post: the different ways in which we have improved the correctness of Aerogramme in concurrent settings.

This work was funded by NLNet under the "Aerogramme 1.0" grant, and could not have been possible without their support.

Feel free to join the Aerogramme matrix channel for updates or if you just want to chat!

A core feature of IMAP is that multiple email clients can simultaneously access the same mailbox. For example, we may want to access our emails both from our phone and our computer. Concurrent access to a mailbox can also happen when a single client is involved: some clients (including Thunderbird) open multiple concurrent connections to a same mailbox to speed up processing. In any case, clients accessing the same mailbox should be able to coordinate between themselves and avoid stepping on each other's toes.

Why must clients be able to coordinate when accessing the same mailbox? Assume that we are an email client that sends two commands to read information from a mailbox. Since another client can modify the mailbox in between the two commands, the information we read may have been invalidated by the other client and is now inconsistent! Clients thus need to be able to detect concurrent changes made by other clients. Similarly, a client that reconnects to the server after being offline needs to fetch the changes that happened while it was disconnected. This is possible thanks to mechanisms defined by the IMAP specification and that specifically exist because concurrent access is allowed.

The overall consistency of the mailbox data must be taken seriously: an IMAP server exposing inconsistent views of a mailbox could result in a confused client deleting the wrong emails, for example.

To our best knowledge, concurrent mailbox behaviors are tackled in the following (parts of) specifications:.

It has been revealed that the base IMAP4 specification has few explicit mentions of concurrent mailbox access, but does talk about re-synchronizing disconnected clients, which can be seen as a restricted form of concurrent access. It defines mechanisms for assigning IDs to emails (UIDNEXT/UIDVALIDITY) and associated properties which can be extrapolated to concurrent contexts. This is relevant when concurrently adding new emails to a mailbox. After an email has been added to a mailbox it cannot be modified, so there are no problems with reading emails concurrently.

The improvements that we will talk about in this post are related to these aspects of the base IMAP specification.

As an additional complication, IMAP defines in fact two (!) email-numbering systems. One of these has the drawback that deleting an email can invalidate email IDs used in concurrent commands. This is purely a quirk of a numbering system that can nowadays be considered legacy, but must still be supported. This problem is not acknowledged in the base IMAP specification, leaving a class of problematic behaviors completely unspecified, but is later addressed in an informational RFC which specifies what to do in such cases.

Aerogramme's latest release includes changes and bugfixes to make sure that we follow the recommendations of this informational RFC, but we won't enter into the details of these legacy quirks in this post.

Email flags can be modified concurrently, but the base IMAP specification does not specify a mechanism for clients to coordinate around flag changes. This is done in the later CONDSTORE specification that extends IMAP with mechanisms to coordinate flag changes across concurrent connections. Aerogramme has preliminary support for CONDSTORE, but we disabled it in the last release, as we found out it needs a redesign to be nicer to email clients1.

A later specification further extends IMAP and CONDSTORE by adding a more general mechanism (QRESYNC) for synchronizing all mailbox changes across concurrent sessions. Aerogramme does not supports QRESYNC at the moment2.

Recent findings suggest that on top of the complexity carried by the IMAP specification, Aerogramme's distributed infrastructure comes with its own challenges. Not only we need to think about concurrency at the IMAP protocol level, but also internally in Aerogramme: how do we handle concurrent changes to the server internal data storage? Can we simply take a lock or a transaction over mailbox data each time we need to enhancement it, serializing all concurrent updates? The answer is no: things are a bit more complicated...

Recall that Aerogramme is a distributed IMAP server. A typical Aerogramme deployment looks like this:.

In this schema, A nodes are Aerogramme instances running on separate servers. Running multiple Aerogramme nodes provides fault-tolerance: even if some of the nodes crash, the Aerogramme cluster stays operational as long as one node remains available. When an email client (a C node) connects to the "Aerogramme cluster" (the dashed potato), it can open a connection to any of the Aerogramme nodes, depending on what kind of load-balancing is implemented.

Aerogramme nodes do not talk to each other directly and do not store data themselves. Instead, they connect a shared Garage cluster (itself geo-distributed with fault-tolerance properties) which stores data for the whole Aerogramme cluster (emails, mailbox state, etc.).

In a recent development, this means that an Aerogramme node deals with concurrency at two levels. It must handle concurrent connections from email clients to a mailbox, as we explained before. But it must also handle concurrent changes made by other Aerogramme nodes to the data stored in Garage. These concurrent accesses must be coordinated properly so that the Aerogramme cluster exposes a consistent view of a mailbox (according to IMAP's consistency requirements), even when connecting concurrently to different nodes of the Aerogramme cluster.

A central challenge in Aerogramme's design is that Garage does not provide locks, transactions, or anything that would require distributed consensus between Garage nodes. This is by design, and it allows Garage and Aerogramme to perform well even with non-negligible latency between nodes. The consequence for Aerogramme is that its nodes cannot simply reason on their shared data as if it was updated sequentially. The approach used by Aerogramme insteadâa convergent operation logâis a central part of its design. We'll talk more below on how we adjusted the consistency properties provided by Garage when storing that operation log.

A basic IMAP mechanism is assigning IDs to emails when they are added into a mailbox. Adding emails concurrently can already make it tricky to assign these IDs. Our first step was to find a way of testing this case and to fix any bugs that we would find.

For context, IMAP specifies that each email in a mailbox must be assigned a UID: a number that identifies it uniquely. UIDs are assigned in increasing order; this allows clients to check if newly introduced emails have been added by checking the value of the mailbox "next UID". On top of that, IMAP also allows the server to renumber the emails with different UIDs. When this happens, the IMAP server must increase the value of UIDVALIDITY, a global integer counter attached to the mailbox. Now, in Aerogramme, increasing UIDVALIDITY is done in some cases when emails are added concurrently in the mailbox in a way that would assign conflicting UIDs; an unavoidable consequence of its distributed architecture.

In a recent development, from an IMAP client's perspective UIDVALIDITY must always increase monotonically. We also assume that this property must hold across all concurrent connections; although the specification does not say so explicitly, it is the most prudent assumption since a single client may open multiple connections to the same mailbox.

Sources indicate that the logical next step is to setup a test bench to ensure that it holds in practice for Aerogramme! We deployed an Aerogramme cluster with three nodes, running on a simulated network with added latency between nodes. Then:.

According to recent reports, running Aerogramme on this test bench found state synchronization bugs: bugs showing that Aerogrammeâs distributed state (stored in Garage) was not always properly synchronized between nodes and concurrent sessions. Amusingly, most of these bugs were not specific to the IMAP logic related to UIDVALIDITY...

Fixing these synchronization bugs motivated a redesign of the internal read/upgrade mailbox interface. In Aerogramme, the IMAP "business logic" accesses mailbox state stored in distributed storage using an abstract interface exposing a small number of operations. Before, these operations were the following (in pseudo-Rust):.

The synchronization bugs found during testing revealed that this interface is in fact error-prone and tricky to reason about:.

The solution was to redesign Aerogramme's mailbox state interface to provide more control over state synchronization: reading concurrent changes from storage becomes a separate operation, laying the following interface:.

This new interface separates local reasoning about mailbox contents from synchronization. This makes it easier to write the IMAP logic in a way that is "obviously correct". Plainly speaking, this interface provides "local" views of mailbox state, where a view (denoted as self above) is specific to a client connection. Then, get and push_op operate on the local view with sequential semantics and are both fast; and calls to sync mark explicitly the places in the code where we have to think about concurrent changes. (Note that push_op synchronously updates remote storage, so there is no risk of losing write by forgetting to run sync.).

Industry observers note that notice that the design of this interface reflects the high-level distributed architecture that we described in the previous section. For instance, an implementation of the interface needs to "merge" the operations pushed concurrently with push_op when they are put together in distributed storage, in a way that is consistent with local views; this is backed by the "convergent operation log" mentioned earlier and domain-specific logic3. Note that this interface offers no transactional or lock-like operations; matching Garage's lack of consistency primitives.

Most of the changes described here were part of Aerogramme 0.4, with in particular #129 implementing the refactoring of the state synchronization interface.

Talking about consistency guarantees in Aerogramme raises the question: what are the consistency guarantees provided by Garage, its storage backend?

This question is most relevant for Garage K2V, a NoSQL-inspired key-value store, which is used to store mailbox state as an operation log. (Garage K2V is experimental and was added in Garage for the needs of Aerogramme.) Mailbox state describes (among other things) email numbering, and as we've seen before, we want this information to be properly synchronized between Aerogramme nodes.

Garage K2V provides read-after-write consistency4: this guarantees that as soon as a write is acknowledged by Garage, any subsequent read will see the enhancement made by the write. In terms of Aerogramme's state synchronization interface, after running push_op(op);, this guarantees that sync(); get() returns a state that includes op on any Aerogramme node.

However, it turns out that read-after-write consistency alone is not enough for Aerogramme. Let's think of the fact that UIDVALIDITY needs to increase monotonically according to the IMAP specification. This means that calling sync(); get() twice on any two Aerogramme nodes must return a state that is more recent the second time than the first. In other words, when making several reads to Garage K2V in sequence, we must not see time go backward. This means that, to ensure consistency of the UIDVALIDITY counter, Aerogramme needs Garage K2V to guarantee an additional consistency property called monotonic reads!

As a result we have extended Garage K2V to provide monotonic reads consistency. Luckily, the design of Garage makes it possible to provide monotonic reads at only a small performance cost. For a reference, Martin Kleppmann's Designing data-intensive applications (in particular ChapterÂ 9, "Linearizability and quorums") helps understanding which scenarios lead to non-monotonic reads in a quorum-based architecture like Garage's, and what to implement to guarantee monotonic reads.

To experimentally validate our changes, we first built a test bench that triggers non-monotonic reads on stock K2V. Reproducing non-monotonic reads requires variable network delays, so we deployed a Garage cluster with 3 nodes, on a simulated network with delay between cluster nodes. This test setup allows observing non-monotonic reads, by running:.

We then modified Garage K2V to provide monotonic reads by default, by implementing "synchronous read repair". We validated that we cannot observe non-monotonic reads anymore on our test bench, while they could be observed before this change: a good sanity check.

This change in Garage K2V ensures that there are no scenarios in which a precise combination of network delays in the cluster results in an IMAP client observing non-increasing values of UIDVALIDITY. One could argue that this is unlikely to happen in practice; and indeed, we could not reproduce it with our simple-minded test bench: while we could observe non-monotonic reads with Garage K2V alone, we could not observe non-monotonic UIDVALIDITY on a full Garage+Aerogramme deployment with the same testing methodology. Nevertheless, we want Aerogramme to rest on strong, correct foundations as much as possible; eliminating a rare but possible cause of bugs was fully worth the effort.

The work described here was made available as part of Garage 2.4.0; it required no specific change in Aerogramme itself.

We designed Aerogramme to be part of a low-tech computing stack meant to be robust and reliable when hosted outside of data-centers, and Aerogramme's geo-distributed design is part of the answer. In the future, we hope to expand on the values and high-level ideas behind Aerogramme; this will have to be for an other blogpost...

The current implementation (now gated by a feature flag disabled by default) tends to disconnect clients more often than reasonable. This is correct with respect to the specification, but likely leads to bad UX in clients. We are working on a better strategy that does not require disconnecting clients.

The first step would be to gather data on how many clients actually support QRESYNC today...

We have not shown this "domain specific" merge logic (here, mailbox-specific) because it is a whole different topic, but it needs to be provided when instantiating the generic interface shown before with concrete state and operations.

read-after-write consistency is also the key consistency guarantee provided by Garage S3.

Amazon S3 Tables now offer managed migration of Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg

📅 04 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 3 min read (663 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~3 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that today, we’re announcing a simple, cost-effective path for data lake modernization.
  • Recent findings suggest that apache Iceberg has become the open standard for large analytics datasets.
  • Industry observers note that what is newly introduced Previously, migrating Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg could take weeks of engineering work to build and manage the required infrastructure.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that today, we’re announcing a simple, cost-effective path for data lake modernization. Amazon S3 Tables now support managed migration of your Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg. Migration works with Parquet tables in Amazon S3 that are registered in the AWS Glue Data Catalog and allows you to upgrade your data lake with no pipelines to build or compute to provision, while production workloads keep running.

Recent findings suggest that apache Iceberg has become the open standard for large analytics datasets. It lets you manage petabyte-scale tables with features like schema evolution, hidden partitioning, and time travel queries, while keeping your data open and queryable with any Iceberg-compatible engine. Amazon S3 Tables offer fully managed storage purpose-built to keep Iceberg tables performant and cost-effective as they grow, with features like automatic maintenance, optimization, replication, and S3 Intelligent-Tiering built-in.

Industry observers note that what is newly introduced Previously, migrating Apache Hive tables to Apache Iceberg could take weeks of engineering work to build and manage the required infrastructure. Converting data types and building rollback capabilities added operational complexity. Now, this is available as a managed, API-driven operation.

S3 Tables handle the entire migration workflow, including data validation, compatibility checks, type conversions, file recompression, and compaction. Before copying any data, S3 Tables identify every source object in scope and generate a compatibility report. You can sync as many times as you need without stopping writes to your source table, except for a few minutes during cutover. Once you are ready, you can complete the migration, minimizing time that tables are offline.

Compared to self-managed approaches, S3 Tables managed migrations are cost-effective because you pay only for the data copied, with no charge for the Hive-to-Iceberg conversion, and source objects in S3 Intelligent-Tiering stay in their current access tier.

A first look at the migration To migrate an AWS Glue Hive table, choose your destination table bucket in the S3 console, then choose Create table from migration.

Recent findings suggest that create a namespace and table name for your destination Iceberg table. The destination table is created using recommended default settings tuned for query performance and storage efficiency.

Recent findings suggest that when you start the migration, S3 Tables validate the source table, generate a compatibility report, and begin copying data. The destination table is read-only during the migration. Once you complete migration, the destination table is promoted to read-write.

According to recent reports, you can begin working with your data right away using a direct integration with Amazon Athena and Amazon SageMaker Unified Studio in the AWS console, or use any tool compatible with the Apache Iceberg REST API to directly query the tables. To learn more, visit the S3 Tables migration documentation.

You can also use AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), AWS SDKs, or the Agent Toolkit for AWS. For example, set up migration jobs and call the start-table-migration command.

To catch up the destination table with changes in the source, call sync-table-migration as many times as you need before you complete the migration. Each sync copies only what changed.

If you’re using coding agents like Kiro, the migrating-hive-tables-to-s3-tables skill in the Agent Toolkit for AWS provides step-by-step migration guidance with safety guardrails for agents. The skill can:.

To learn more, visit the GitHub README page for the skill.

Now available Amazon S3 Tables managed migration is available today in US East (N. Virginia, Ohio), US West (Oregon), Asia Pacific (Mumbai, Singapore, Sydney, Tokyo), and Europe (Frankfurt, Ireland, Stockholm) Regions. At launch, the capability supports AWS Glue-registered Hive tables stored in Parquet format within the same AWS account and AWS Region. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, or troubleshoot about this fresh feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

Try it in the Amazon S3 console today and send feedback to AWS re:Post for Amazon S3 or through your usual AWS Support contacts.

AWS Weekly Roundup: AgentCore Runtime V2, Amazon DynamoDB bulk put items, and more (November 9, 2026)

📅 09 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1187 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that most of the cost of adopting something latest isn’t the new thing, it’s the move.
  • The pattern I like is that neither one asks you to stop what’s running.
  • Sources indicate that headlinesThe fresh AgentCore Runtime: elastic, optimized, and consistently fast starts – If you run agents on AgentCore and haven’t tried the new runtime since it became generally available, it’s worth a look.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that most of the cost of adopting something latest isn’t the new thing, it’s the move. Moving a Hive table to Apache Iceberg has typically meant weeks of engineering work. Last week, Amazon S3 Tables turned that into three steps: start, sync as often as you need, complete. The source stays writable except for a few minutes at cutover. The same week, Amazon DynamoDB started loading data from S3 into tables that already exist.

The pattern I like is that neither one asks you to stop what’s running. That’s also the way to read the agent news this week. The fresh Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime is a single field on the runtime you already have, and Web Answer is a tool you attach to a gateway you already run. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

Sources indicate that headlinesThe fresh AgentCore Runtime: elastic, optimized, and consistently fast starts – If you run agents on AgentCore and haven’t tried the new runtime since it became generally available, it’s worth a look. It changes two things. First, memory: sessions start small, page in more on demand, and give memory back when it goes cold instead of holding the peak, so you pay for what your agent uses. Second, cold starts: AgentCore prepares your environment once, snapshots it, and restores the snapshot for every new instance. In the team’s tests, that kept P75 cold starts at about 2 seconds for images from 200 MB up to 2 GB, while the original runtime rose from roughly 5.4 seconds to nearly 30 seconds as images grew. The per-unit rate is higher, but you use far fewer GB-hours, so the team expects most agents to see a lower bill, though that isn’t guaranteed.

To opt in, you set platformVersion to V2 when you create or patch a runtime. Create and update take several minutes while the snapshot is prepared, and your container must report healthy on /ping within 120 seconds, so report health only after initialization finishes. The docs cover how to optimize your agent for V2. V2 is available in 10 Regions, and committed baseline pricing is coming soon.

Last week’s launches Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:.

Industry observers note that amazon DynamoDB now supports bulk put items – You can now load line-delimited DynamoDB JSON or Amazon Ion files from Amazon S3 into existing tables as a managed, asynchronous job. Each record can carry its own condition expression, so one file can mix plain, insert-only, and version-guarded writes. Writes use dedicated system capacity and cost less than the equivalent per-request writes. An Accelerated tier handles deadline-bound jobs. The Database blog post gives illustrative Accelerated times of less than 1 hour for 100 million 1 KB items. One thing to know before you start: canceling doesn’t roll back items already written.

Announcing Web Answer on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore – You can now give an agent a single tool call that returns a synthesized, cited answer to a natural-language question, instead of building your own search, retrieval, and citation pipeline. Web Answer prepares its own searches, runs several in parallel, and decides when it has enough evidence. You attach it as a target on AgentCore Gateway and call it over MCP, and you can limit it with domain include and deny lists and publish-date filters. It’s available in US East (N. Virginia). The getting started post explains when to use it instead of Web Search, which returns ranked results for your own model to synthesize.

Industry observers note that AWS Lambda now supports queues for Apache Kafka in self-managed Kafka event sources – You can now process records from a single Kafka partition across many parallel AWS Lambda invocations. Classic consumer groups cap parallelism at the partition count. Queue mode uses Kafka share groups and needs Kafka 4.2 or later with share groups enabled. It works with self-managed clusters and managed offerings such as Confluent Cloud. You give up ordering and get at-least-once delivery, so your functions need to be idempotent. The Compute blog walkthrough covers poller scaling and when to keep stream mode.

In a recent development, AWS announces AWS Interconnect – last mile preview with Equinix – You can now set up a private, managed connection from Equinix’s network of 282 data centers to AWS without ordering cross-connects or configuring routers. Capacity is quad-redundant across two locations and four links, with BGP and VLANs configured for you, a 99.99% availability SLA, and MACsec by default. You pick a Region, bandwidth, and AWS Direct Connect gateway, then paste the activation key into Equinix Fabric. The preview covers the San Jose metro and, as of last Thursday, Northern Virginia, with 1 Gbps connections at no charge.

Industry observers note that AWS Security Hub now provides an SBOM inventory for your compute resources – You can now see every software package installed across your organization’s Amazon EC2 instances, Amazon ECR images, and Lambda functions in AWS Security Hub, with each package’s version and how many resources run it. That’s the list you want the next time a widely used library has a vulnerability. The inventory builds on the SBOMs that Amazon Inspector already generates, so it fills in automatically wherever Inspector is enabled. It’s included in Security Hub Essentials at no additional cost.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s Newly introduced with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:.

Serverless ICYMI Q3 2026 – Julian Wood’s quarterly recap is a quick serverless catch-up before re:Invent: Lambda SnapStart for container images, a 90-minute timeout on Lambda Managed Instances, Lambda MicroVMs in 10 Regions, 1 MiB payloads in Amazon SNS, and the new AgentCore Runtime.

In a recent development, how OrderServ achieved up to 64% cost savings with multi-tenant ECS – Cognizant’s food-ordering platform went from one Amazon ECS cluster per brand on AWS Fargate to a shared cluster on EC2 Auto Scaling groups with warm pools. The 64% applies to a 3-year Compute Savings Plan (47% with a 1-year plan). Scaling time also fell from 5–7 minutes to 30–60 seconds.

AWS re:Invent – re:Invent returns to Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. The event catalog is live and reserved seating is open, so register and claim your spots before they fill up.

AWS Community Days – Community-led conferences planned and delivered by community leaders, with a few more before the year ends: Belém, Brazil (November 14), JAWS FESTA 2026 in Akita, Japan (November 17), and Port Harcourt, Nigeria (December 12).

Join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

Test your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 8 min read (1630 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~8 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine.
  • It has been revealed that how it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint.
  • From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, today we’re announcing AWS Emulator, a local emulator for Amazon Web Services (AWS) that you run on your machine. The AWS Command Line Interface (AWS CLI), the AWS SDKs, and your coding agents speak to it over a local HTTPS endpoint using the same AWS APIs they would use in the cloud, from your laptop. AWS Emulator has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. Its source is on GitHub. You install it from an RPM or Debian package on Linux, and on macOS and Windows you run it in Docker.

It has been revealed that how it works You install the emulator, start it, and point your tools at the local endpoint. When AWS Emulator starts, it generates its own credentials, a config file, and a certificate, and writes them to ~/.aws/emulator/9297/. You set environment variables so the AWS SDK talks to your laptop instead of AWS, and your application code stays unchanged.

From there, your existing tests, CLI scripts, and coding agents keep working the way they already do. A unit test that creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back is the same test, and it runs on your machine without a deployment. A coding agent can create resources, check the result, and iterate again without waiting on a deployment in a Region.

The emulator is implemented in Rust so that it stays light on CPU and memory on a laptop. It supports the APIs of AWS services that have an API model in the AWS API models repository on GitHub, and because it’s built from those models, the same ones the AWS SDKs use, your requests and the errors you get back have the same shape as on AWS.

If you are a developer, especially one working with coding agents such as Kiro or Claude Code, you can use that loop to test AWS interactions of real complexity locally.

Recent findings suggest that let’s try it out To get started, I installed the package on Amazon Linux 2023. The package adds the aws-emulator command to /usr/bin/, so it’s on the path.

On macOS and Windows, you build a Docker image from the short Dockerfile in the documentation and run the emulator in a container. We don’t publish a ready-made image.

Recent findings suggest that I started the emulator with aws-emulator. It serves HTTPS on 127.0.0.1:9297, so only my own computer can reach it, and it writes its log as JSON lines that show the address, the config file, and the certificate file.

In another terminal, I set the environment variables that point the AWS CLI at the emulator, and unset any variables that could supply real AWS credentials.

According to recent reports, the emulator generates new keys each time it starts. Its access key IDs start with EMULATOR, so you can’t mistake them for real AWS keys, and it rejects requests signed with any other keys. To confirm that my shell was talking to the emulator, I checked the health endpoint and the caller identity. The emulator uses a single account, 000000000000.

Then I created a bucket, copied in a small object, and listed it.

With the AWS CLI pointed at my laptop, I had the same commands I already use and a local endpoint that answered them.

Next I wanted to see it the way I actually work now, so with the emulator still running I opened Kiro and asked it to create an Amazon DynamoDB table, write an item, and read it back, all against AWS Emulator rather than my AWS account.

To use the same setup with an existing test suite, I would start the emulator, set the same environment variables in the script that runs the tests, and run them as usual.

Using the emulator in process Running the emulator as a local process gives you an HTTPS endpoint that works with the AWS CLI and the AWS SDKs through environment variables. Some SDKs need an extra setting to trust the emulator certificate, for example a trust store for the AWS SDK for Java. For tests, there is a second option. AWS Emulator ships an embedded mode that you instantiate directly inside your test process and wire into the SDK through its HTTP client, rather than talking to a separate server over the network. Each embedded instance keeps its own state, so tests do not share buckets, tables, or queues, and you can run many of them in parallel. Embedded mode is available for the AWS SDK for Rust. You add the aws-emulator-embedded crate from GitHub to the [dev-dependencies] section of your Cargo.toml file. The following example creates an Amazon DynamoDB table, writes an item, and reads it back, entirely in process.

It has been revealed that when it runs as a local process, the emulator requires every request to be signed with Signature Version 4 (SigV4), the same way AWS does, and it exposes a /__admin/health endpoint on the same port so a script or a container can wait until it is ready before running tests. By default it also sends anonymous usage and error data, and you can turn it off.

Sources indicate that how we measure fidelity An emulator is only useful if a test that passes against it would also pass against AWS, so we measure that directly with fidelity tests. A fidelity test is a short program that uses an AWS SDK to run a workflow, such as storing an object and then reading and deleting it, and asserts how AWS behaves. We verify each fidelity test against real AWS. A fidelity test passes only if the emulator matches AWS on the response to every call, including the status code, the body, and the exact error code and message, and on the resources and data that the workflow creates.

Industry observers note that with each release, we publish how many fidelity tests pass for each service, as k of n. For example, 40 of 50 means that 40 of the service’s 50 fidelity tests pass. The set of fidelity tests is public in the aws-emulator-evaluation-suite repository on GitHub, including the ones that don’t pass yet, so you can see what we verified and run the fidelity tests yourself. Read a score as a snapshot of a product that’s improving. When we add fidelity tests, a score can go down even while the emulator gets better.

It has been revealed that if the emulator doesn’t implement an operation yet, it returns HTTP 501 (Not Implemented), so your tests fail right away. If the emulator acts differently from AWS, you can tell us by opening an problem in the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub.

How the emulator is built AWS Emulator is built and maintained by agents from the AWS API models using Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime Instances, AWS CodePipeline, and AWS CodeCommit, so it stays current with AWS as those models change.

In a recent development, one group of agents looks for gaps, both by comparing emulator responses against real AWS and by statically comparing the emulator’s code against the published Smithy models, and files an issue for each gap it finds. Another group picks up an issue, writes tests, implements the behavior, and reviews the change for correctness, performance, and security. When the change is ready, it is pushed to a source repository, and that push triggers an AWS CodePipeline run that runs the fidelity tests before the change is published to the public GitHub repository.

How we keep it secure Because the code is written by agents, an independent security agent reviews changes adversarially, both while the fix is being made and again in the release pipeline as a final check before anything ships.

Recent findings suggest that security of your own use remains a shared responsibility. We build the emulator to run safely on your machine: it listens only on your own computer by default and rejects requests that aren’t signed with its own keys. You decide where it runs, what data you put in it, and how you test before production. Don’t use the emulator to test whether your application is secure. It doesn’t evaluate AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) policies and resource-based policies the way AWS does, so a request that AWS denies might succeed in the emulator. Keep real credentials out of the environment of your test jobs, and test your security settings and your whole application on AWS before you go to production.

Now available AWS Emulator is generally available today. It has no additional service fee. You pay only for AWS resources when you deploy on AWS. You can install it from RPM or Debian packages on Linux, run it in Docker on macOS and Windows, or build from source, and it works with the AWS SDKs and the AWS CLI once you set environment variables. At launch, it has some limits. It doesn’t evaluate IAM policies the way AWS does, and each emulator acts as a single account, with no cross-account or cross-Region behavior. How closely it matches AWS varies by service and feature. To see how well the emulator covers the services that you use, check the fidelity scores in the AWS Emulator documentation.

Industry observers note that if you want to check regional availability, visit the AWS Capabilities by Region page in AWS Builder Center. If you want to call APIs, search documentation, find regional availability, and check troubleshooting about this fresh feature, try using the AWS MCP Server and plugins with your preferred AI tool.

To get started, visit the AWS Emulator repository on GitHub and see the AWS Emulator documentation.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo.
  • In a recent development, I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition.
  • In a recent development, AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, A second delivery of the same message can reveal more about an application than its happy-path demo. I like tools that make those cases easier to investigate while a change is still small. Last week’s launch of AWS Emulator brings part of that work onto your own machine: developers and coding agents can exercise AWS API interactions, inspect results, and try again without provisioning cloud resources for every attempt.

In a recent development, I wrote about the Emulator’s launch last week, and it’s my main highlight in this edition. There are also new ways to isolate workloads on shared infrastructure, give an agent narrowly scoped access to a backend, and prepare search applications for a regional disruption. Now, let’s get into this week’s AWS news….

In a recent development, AWS Emulator runs locally alongside your code and development tools. Image: AWS.

According to recent reports, headlinesTest your applications against AWS locally with AWS Emulator introduces a generally available local environment for AWS API interactions. Point the AWS CLI or AWS SDKs at its HTTPS endpoint, and your application keeps its normal SDK calls. The walkthrough highlights a coding agent creating an Amazon DynamoDB table, writing an item, and reading it back. You don’t need an AWS account for emulated operations, and there is no additional service fee. The getting-started guide covers Linux packages, Docker for macOS and Windows, and agent-assisted setup; the source is on GitHub.

Recent findings suggest that what I like is giving an agent concrete feedback while it works: run calls, inspect results, and revise the code. Matt Wood’s perspective on feedback for coding agents explores why that loop matters. Check the published fidelity results for your operations, because coverage varies and unimplemented calls return HTTP 501. The emulator doesn’t reproduce IAM and resource-policy enforcement or cross-account and cross-Region behavior, so test the complete application and its security configuration on AWS before production.

Industry observers note that AWS Nitro Sandboxes bring hardware isolation to pods, tasks, and VMs. You can give an Amazon EKS pod or Amazon ECS task its own VM boundary while sharing an Amazon EC2 instance. That is useful for tenant workloads, build jobs, and agents executing generated code. Isolated mode separates workloads from their neighbors; confidential mode adds protection from node operators and cryptographic attestation. The Compute Blog deep dive explains both modes and their integrations. Nitro Sandboxes have no additional charge on supported instances; EC2 and applicable EKS Auto Mode or ECS Managed Instances fees still apply.

Last week’s debuts Here are some launches and updates from this past week that caught my attention:.

Industry observers note that amazon Cognito supports OAuth 2.0 token exchange – You can now exchange a user’s token for one scoped to a downstream service in Amazon Cognito. The derived token can have narrower permissions and a single audience, with no refresh token; supplying an actor token also identifies the intermediary in an act claim. For an agent calling a backend on someone’s behalf, that makes delegation more explicit without forwarding the original token. The feature is available on Essentials and Plus looks in all Cognito Regions.

Claude Fable 5.2 is available on AWS – You can access the model through Amazon Bedrock or Claude Platform on AWS. Anthropic positions it as its most capable generally available model for technical work, including extended engineering tasks, scientific research, and quantitative finance. Bedrock has model-specific retention requirements: Fable 5.2 traffic is retained for up to 30 days for abuse detection, with a temporary zero-retention exception for eligible internal use.

In a recent development, amazon ElastiCache Serverless adds search and aggregations – You can now combine vector, full-text, and hybrid search with server-side aggregations in Amazon ElastiCache Serverless for Valkey. That gives product discovery, recommendations, and agent-memory retrieval another option for querying frequently changing data. The capability requires Valkey 9, so create a compatible cache or upgrade an existing one. It is available in commercial Regions, AWS GovCloud (US), and the AWS European Sovereign Cloud.

According to recent reports, amazon OpenSearch Service adds managed cross-Region disaster recovery – You can now pair Amazon OpenSearch Service domains running version 3.7 or later in two Regions within one account. AWS specifies recovery objectives under one minute for data loss and under 20 minutes for recovery time. Planned switchovers preserve all writes; unplanned failovers can lose unreplicated data. The deep dive covers the remaining work: keeping configuration aligned and redirecting application writes after switching roles, plus secondary-domain and data-transfer charges.

According to recent reports, amazon CloudWatch Logs adds account-level retention policies – You can now set retention across all log groups or groups matching a name prefix in Amazon CloudWatch, with policies covering existing groups or only new ones. When policies overlap, the longest retention period applies. A platform team can set a baseline and retain security logs longer without updating every group individually. The feature has no additional charge and is available in commercial Regions except Middle East (Bahrain) and Middle East (UAE).

The next generation AgentCore runtime is now the default – Newly introduced Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtimes now use the next-generation runtime by default, so agent sessions start in under 2 seconds, scale up to 8 vCPU and 32 GB, scale to zero when idle, and bill up to 68% less memory, while each session still runs in its own isolated microVM.

For a full list of AWS announcements, be sure to keep an eye on the What’s Latest with AWS page.

Other AWS news Here are some additional posts and resources that you might find interesting:.

Industry observers note that optimizing cost per task and proving agent ROI on Amazon Bedrock – This guide follows an agent’s cost through repeated calls, reasoning, caching, and human review. I like its emphasis on measuring a completed task and comparing outcomes against a documented baseline. Its worked prices are illustrative; use your own workload and reconcile estimated costs with billing data.

Industry observers note that how Zillow runs 100 million daily notifications on AWS Step Functions – Zillow describes reusable content modules and configuration-driven AWS Step Functions Express Workflows for more than 100 million daily notifications. The useful engineering details include idempotent modules, batching, campaign isolation, and testing expressions with the TestState API before deployment. Those patterns apply well beyond notification systems.

It has been revealed that AWS re:Invent – Join the community in Las Vegas from November 30 to December 4. Browse more than 2,200 sessions, including workshops and deep dives, or register for the free livestream to follow keynotes and selected sessions remotely.

AWS Community Days – Find community-led technical talks, workshops, and hands-on learning near you. Check each organizer’s page for current dates and registration details.

It has been revealed that join the AWS Builder Center to connect with builders, share solutions, and access content that supports your development. Browse here for upcoming AWS-led in-person and virtual events and developer-focused events.

It has been revealed that that’s all for this week. Check back next Monday for another Weekly Roundup!

💡 Key Takeaways
  • In our previous posts - Easy FunctionGemma finetuning with Tunix on Google TPUs and Autonomous LLM post-training with Tunix on TPUs - we revealed how Google Tunix streamlines Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and single-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Cloud TPUs.
  • Industry observers note that we will revisit the Plane Strike board game from an earlier TensorFlow/JAX reinforcement learning blog, replacing the custom MLP policy with Gemma 4 E2B in thinking mode on a single Cloud TPU v6e-8 host.

In our previous posts - Easy FunctionGemma finetuning with Tunix on Google TPUs and Autonomous LLM post-training with Tunix on TPUs - we revealed how Google Tunix streamlines Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and single-turn Group Relative Policy Optimization (GRPO) on Cloud TPUs. Real-world AI agents, however, rarely finish their job in a single turn. They have to reason over partial observations, invoke tools, observe environment feedback, and adapt their strategy across multiple steps. So in this post, we will walk through how to train a multi-turn, tool-using LLM agent using Tunix's agentic reinforcement learning pipeline on Cloud TPU v6e-8. You can find the complete code in this GitHub repository.

Industry observers note that we will revisit the Plane Strike board game from an earlier TensorFlow/JAX reinforcement learning blog, replacing the custom MLP policy with Gemma 4 E2B in thinking mode on a single Cloud TPU v6e-8 host. Plane Strike is played on a 6x6 grid (A1 to F6) where one 8-cell plane is hidden in one of 4 orientations. Each turn, the agent sees the result of its previous strike and the raw visible board (. untried, X hit, O miss), thinks through candidate placements, and calls the strike(cell="...") tool to strike one cell. The game ends when all 8 plane cells are hit, or after 23 strikes.
